items.title: CAN 2025 : le TAS ouvre le dossier explosif Maroc-Sénégal le 8 octobre
items.description: Dix mois après la finale controversée de la CAN 2025, remportée sur le terrain par le Sénégal face au Maroc (1-0), le litige entre les deux sélections s’apprête à connaître une nouvelle étape décisive devant le Tribunal arbitral du sport (TAS), basé à Lausanne, en Suisse. Selon RMC Sport, le jury d’appel de la Confédération africaine de football (CAF) avait, en mars dernier, décidé d’attribuer la victoire au Maroc sur tapis vert, à la suite des incidents survenus lors de la finale. Une décision contestée par la partie sénégalaise, qui a saisi le TAS afin de faire réexaminer l’affaire. Le dossier sera examiné par une formation arbitrale présidée par le professeur français Gérald Simon. Il sera assisté de l’Italien Luigi Fumagalli et de l’Allemand Ulrich Haas, deux autres spécialistes du droit du sport. L’audience est prévue le 8 octobre prochain à partir de 9h30 au siège du TAS. Toutefois, la décision ne devrait pas être rendue le jour même. Le tribunal devra prendre le temps d’examiner les arguments des différentes parties avant de rendre sa sentence. L’issue de cette procédure déterminera donc définitivement le sort de la finale de la CAN 2025 et, par conséquent, celui du trophée attribué à l’issue de la compétition.

items.title: Foot: L'AS FAR ambitionne de briller sur tous les fronts
items.description: L’AS FAR entend jouer les premiers rôles sur tous les fronts cette saison, a souligné le nouvel entraîneur du club militaire, Pedro Gonçalves, affichant de solides ambitions en Botola Pro D1 « Inwi » comme sur la scène continentale, où son équipe est engagée en Coupe de la Confédération africaine de football (CAF). « Nous devons nous battre dans toutes les compétitions dans lesquelles nous sommes engagés », a affirmé le technicien portugais dans un entretien accordé à la MAP, quelques jours après le lancement de la nouvelle saison, marquée notamment par le report du choc de la première journée entre l’AS FAR et le Raja de Casablanca. Pour Pedro Gonçalves, le statut de l’AS FAR impose cette ambition. « L’AS FAR est une référence, non seulement au Maroc, mais sur le continent », a-t-il souligné, mettant en avant la responsabilité qui accompagne cette dimension. Le technicien portugais veut, ainsi, construire un groupe capable de répondre aux exigences d’un calendrier chargé et de rester compétitif sur l’ensemble des tableaux. « Nous avons beaucoup de matchs à disputer durant la saison. L’opportunité viendra donc pour tout le monde », a-t-il relevé, insistant sur l’importance d’un effectif suffisamment étoffé pour gérer les différentes échéances. En championnat, l’objectif reste particulièrement élevé. Après plusieurs saisons à la lutte pour le titre, l’AS FAR entend, une nouvelle fois, jouer les premiers rôles. « Notre grand objectif reste le championnat », a affirmé Pedro Gonçalves, faisant de la Botola Pro D1 « Inwi » l’une des principales priorités de la saison. Sur la scène continentale, l’AS FAR devra cette fois défendre ses ambitions en Coupe de la Confédération. Une compétition que le technicien portugais considère majeure, malgré la non-participation du club à la Ligue des Champions. « C’est une compétition très importante », a-t-il souligné, en référence également au parcours continental réalisé par l’AS FAR la saison dernière, marqué par une finale de la compétition interclubs africaine phare. Pedro Gonçalves sait, toutefois, que le contexte africain impose des exigences particulières. Les longs déplacements, les changements de climat, la diversité des styles de jeu et les réalités propres à chaque pays constituent autant d'aléas auxquels son équipe devra s’adapter. Le technicien mise, dans ce contexte, sur un groupe mêlant expérience et jeunesse. Une grande partie de l’effectif de la saison dernière a été conservée, alors que plusieurs recrues ont rejoint le club durant l’intersaison. Cette continuité doit faciliter l’intégration des nouveaux joueurs dans un collectif déjà structuré. Elle permet également au staff de travailler sur des bases connues, tout en introduisant progressivement de nouvelles idées. Après près de deux mois de préparation, Pedro Gonçalves se dit satisfait de l’évolution de son groupe. Il reconnaît, toutefois, que l’adaptation reste nécessaire, notamment pour les joueurs venus de l’étranger et les jeunes éléments issus de la Botola. Le départ de Mohamed Rabie Hrimat constitue, par ailleurs, l’un des principaux changements de l’intersaison. Le technicien portugais a salué le parcours de l’ancien capitaine, tout en estimant que son départ ouvre une nouvelle étape pour l’équipe. Avec un effectif étoffé, la concurrence interne devrait également jouer un rôle important. Le calendrier chargé doit permettre au technicien de faire appel à l’ensemble de ses joueurs et de maintenir le groupe mobilisé tout au long de la saison. L’AS FAR aborde, ainsi, l’exercice avec une ambition globale… Rester compétitive en Botola, aller le plus loin possible en Coupe de la Confédération et répondre présente à chaque rendez-vous de la saison. items.title: Why Americans Stopped Throwing Dinner Parties
items.description: M id-century Americans knew how to throw a party, for better or worse. In some of the most famous titles of the 1950s and 1960s— Couples , by John Updike; Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf? , by Edward Albee; Revolutionary Road , by Richard Yates—the drama (and martini-soaked melodrama) took place in middle-class living rooms. The stories were fictional, but the setting was realistic. Until 1975, half of Americans said they entertained guests at their home every month. Then something changed. Americans stopped throwing parties. Even more fundamental, they stopped visiting one another. From 1975 to 1998, the share of Americans who gave or attended a monthly dinner party declined by half. The share of Americans saying they never entertained people at home tripled. Although cultural critics often bemoan the decline of organized religion, the dip in church attendance was downright modest compared with the collapse in hosting, according to data gathered by the DDB Needham Life Style Surveys. In his 2000 book, Bowling Alone , Robert Putnam wrote that if these trends continued, the ancient practice of visiting with friends “might entirely disappear from American life in less than a generation.” Check your calendars. One generation and change later, Putnam’s prediction needs an update. S o what’s the state of hosting in the 21st century? To get an apples-to-apples answer to that question, the polling group Data for Progress replicated the DDB Needham Life Style Surveys cited by Putnam. Unfortunately, the upshot is about as brutal as you’d imagine. In the past 30 years, Americans have seen double-digit declines in practically every measure of socializing. They are less likely to play cards; attend a sporting event; go to the bar; volunteer; work on a community project. [ Read: Americans need to party more ] When it comes to hosting people at home, the declines are particularly stark. Since 1995, the share of Americans who say they’ve hosted guests or attended a dinner party has declined by about 20 percent, from 88 to 67 percent—and that’s in addition to the declines that Putnam noted a quarter century ago. Combining the two surveys, we get this astonishing fact: The share of Americans who say they host friends or family at their home at least monthly has fallen from 42 percent in 1975 to 12 percent in 2026—a 70 percent collapse in a half century. To figure out what’s going on, let’s first reject a few stories that don’t entirely fit the data. Perhaps, an optimist might think, Americans are hosting fewer dinner parties because they’ve simply moved all of their hangouts to restaurants and bars. Nice idea, but almost certainly wrong. As Putnam wrote in his book, “the practice of entertaining friends has not simply moved outside the home, but seems to be vanishing entirely.” Overall face-to-face socializing has declined significantly in the past few decades, and the restaurant industry has actually noted a sharp increase in people eating alone. Another plausible theory is that Americans have replaced dinner parties with other forms of healthy socialization. Americans do engage in some activities much more frequently than in 1975, such as going to concerts, traveling, and exercising. All very good. But the evidence suggests that, despite the increase in running clubs, the surge in exercise time seems to be mostly solo. A lot of people are going to the gym with a podcast to keep them company or rolling out a yoga mat in the basement. Most important, it is impossible to assert that Americans are getting out of the house to socialize in new ways when time spent at home has certifiably exploded since the 2010s. I n short, the great disinvitation is real, and we can’t wish or explain it away by arguing that Americans are just finding new ways to be with friends. Here are four explanations: First is that people are more harried, especially those in dual-earner households. In the 1970 book The Harried Leisure Class , the Swedish economist Staffan Burenstam Linder wrote that as a society gets richer, leisure time takes on the frantic quality of work, because each hour of downtime practically shouts, Excuse me! You could be making money right now! We multitask and pack various activities into short periods. Firing up a Netflix show at 9 p.m. that you can half ignore while you answer email is a perfect activity for people who need their leisure time to feel like half-productive box-checking. Taking several hours to coordinate with other busy people to set up a lengthy dinner party is a tougher sell. That’s a sociological explanation, but the decline of hosting is also about macroeconomic trends. In Bowling Alone , Putnam acknowledged that women have historically been the keepers of the family social calendar, planning the birthday parties and neighborhood potlucks. For any number of reasons, women seem to do better than men at making and keeping adult friendships and making plans with other families. But in the 1950s and 1960s, tens of millions of women traded their unpaid household-management jobs for salaried jobs, and the family social calendar frayed, as men failed to pick up the slack. Moving from macro to micro: My wife and I love to host parties. But these get-togethers are a lot of work: conception, communication, coordination, shopping. Are your kids coming, or are you getting a babysitter? Does your eldest kid eat eggplant? No? We’ll make pasta. Oh, that’s right, your wife’s gluten allergy … These multiskilled logistical adventures are almost indistinguishable from the sort of logistical problem-solving that characterizes a good deal of white-collar work. But when both parents are already inundated with literal white-collar work, it’s hard to add the job of unpaid party planner. The trouble with going all in on this explanation—beyond the fact that it embraces a version of learned helplessness for men—is that leisure time has increased overall since the 1950s. Theoretically, married couples should have even more time to have people over for food and drink. Other facts must be squeezing out socializing. Another possibility is that intensive parenting leaves less time for hosting. Americans used to have many kids whom they cared for sparsely; now they have fewer children to whom they devote every minute of their life. The numbers here are unreal. The sociologists Liana C. Sayer, Suzanne M. Bianchi, and John P. Robinson wrote in 2004 that from 1975 to 1998, mothers increased the amount of time they spent with their kids by about 200 minutes a week. In the 21st century, mothering time has continued to rise. For married fathers, parenting time increased by even more. Thus evenings that adults once spent hosting adults are now spent holding, bathing, driving, tutoring, playing with, and talking to their children. A third explanation is that friendship networks are shrinking, especially for poor people who aren’t married. If you’re going to throw a dinner party, you probably need a few things first. Say, a dinner table. Chairs. Food and drink. And also: friends. It is rare to host a dinner party for people you’ve never met. But the average number of close friendships is declining with each generation, and the decline is steepest for Americans without a college degree. So it’s not just that married people have fewer dinner parties; poor people, who are less likely to be married, have fewer friends, period. According to Data for Progress, the two groups most likely to say they never entertained people in their home in the previous year were political independents (44 percent) and people without a college diploma (39 percent). The latter isn’t surprising, given all of the evidence that socializing is declining most rapidly among poorer Americans with less education. Hosting friends, like so much socializing, is in danger of becoming a luxury good. The political wrinkle is more intriguing to me. I sometimes hear from people who tie everything back to politics that political polarization might lead to social fragmentation. But I wonder if the opposite is just as plausible. Maybe people who are less embedded in strong social networks are less likely to attach themselves to groups of all kinds, including political parties. In this way, America’s long-term detachment from groups and institutions is leading to a kind of pox-on-all-parties mentality that cashes out in an increase in independents. [ From the February 2025 issue: The anti-social century ] A final possibility is that it’s too much fun to be home alone. The rise of aloneness is arguably the product of mostly positive trends. In the 20th century, perhaps, many housewives planned dinner parties out of a feeling of crushing isolation. Americans felt suffocating social pressure to attend social events with neighbors and fellow congregants whom they hated. Now we are free to be exactly who and where we want to be. For many, this freedom has taken the shape of a living-room couch. The average time that Americans spent at home increased by almost two hours a day from 2003 to 2022. Cocooned within personalized entertainment fortresses, more Americans have shrunk the great buffet of all possible leisure activities to the small plate of screened media. Something deep in the human psyche seems to want to turn off our self-talk and silence our nattering internal monologues by turning up the volume of other characters’ voices. T he death of the host is the story of lonely unmarried people and harried married dual-earner households, anxious parents spending more time with their children and less time with friends, and the typical home becoming such a riot of diverting comfort that people no longer have to invite human beings to interrupt their boredom. For 200 years, people have worried that machines would make human labor unnecessary. This false assumption is commonly known as the “lump of labor” fallacy. (The finiteness of the labor market is the fallacy here, because people keep finding new problems to turn into jobs.) But machines in the past half century have accomplished something stranger. They have made other people less necessary to our leisure. Every generation has acquired better ways to entertain itself without leaving the house. The result is a peculiar triumph of modern abundance: We have built a world in which being alone has never been easier, more comfortable, or more fun. And then we wonder why everybody stopped coming over. Leisure, as an activity to be enjoyed with other people, turns out to be more finite than work. The lump-of-labor fallacy was wrong, because technology keeps failing to replace jobs. But the “lump of leisure” theory might be right on the money. Social leisure turns out to be the real lump—something finite and easily displaced by technology. Our technology keeps getting better. Our social lives keep getting smaller. Is this what we want? It depends on what want means. Everybody might prefer, in the abstract, a world of dinner parties, neighborhood friendships, and spontaneous gatherings. But on any given Wednesday at 7:45 p.m., looking at a screen is easier than hosting a party. This is not so much an individual failure as a coordination failure. Modernity has shifted leisure from activities that require coordination with other people toward activities that can be consumed without the permission or participation of others. Compared with TikTok, a dinner party is a terrible leisure technology. It requires matching schedules, cleaning the house, buying food, accommodating children and allergies, tolerating awkwardness, and taking the risk that the evening is mediocre. By contrast, what does television ask of us? Nothing. TikTok? Even less. We keep creating opportunities for downtime that eliminate the need for other people to be present. Not all progress is progress. This article was adapted from a post on Derek Thompson’s Substack.

items.title: The Problem With Trump’s Crime Claims
items.description: P resident Trump is deeply unpopular , and his party is on track to lose badly in the midterm elections. But at least one thing is going well on his watch: The nation’s homicide rate has dropped to its lowest level since at least 1900, and the number of violent crimes is falling across the country at the fastest pace ever recorded. Trump and senior administration officials, including the domestic-policy adviser Stephen Miller, are celebrating these trends as the effect of their immigration crackdown at the southern border and on U.S. streets. “Before I took office, we had the worst and most dangerous border on Earth,” Trump asserted to the United Nations General Assembly last week. Now, he said, no one is allowed into the United States unless they’re invited. “As a result, last year we achieved the largest drop in violent crime ever recorded.” The president had been even more explicit at an August rally in South Carolina. “If you wanna get the migrant criminals out of your communities, you have to vote Republican,” he said. ICE arrested about 50,000 immigrants a month this summer, the highest level ever, and deportations are on track for a record year. But Trump’s claim about ICE’s role in the falling crime rate is not backed up by his own administration’s data. Several of the cities and states that have seen the sharpest drops in the homicide rate, according to FBI and census data, are also the “ sanctuary jurisdictions ” that the administration deplores as incubators of violent crime. (The Department of Justice defines sanctuary jurisdictions as places with “policies, laws, or regulations that impede enforcement of federal immigration laws.” Those jurisdictions have adopted policies that limit cooperation between their police departments and ICE.) Three of the five jurisdictions that recorded the largest change in the violent-crime rate, according to FBI and census data, were labeled sanctuaries: Connecticut, Illinois, and the District of Columbia. And of the 11 states where the homicide rate is falling fastest, six are considered sanctuary jurisdictions by the DOJ: Vermont, Delaware, Maryland, Illinois, Washington State and New York. Another—Massachusetts—has a sanctuary policy in its largest city. Similarly, the states with the highest numbers of ICE arrests do not have the largest decreases in violent crime, either in terms of raw numbers or as a percentage change compared with last year. Georgia has been consistently among the top 10 states for monthly ICE arrests, according to federal data analyzed by the Deportation Data Project at the University of California. But FBI and census data rank Georgia 33rd in the violent-crime-rate reduction. Virginia, which has also consistently been in the top 10 for ICE arrests over the past year, is 34th among states in falling violent-crime rates. And although Florida consistently has had the second- or third-highest number of monthly ICE arrests over the past year, it was 18th among states for its violent-crime-rate drop. To be sure, there are cities with relatively high numbers of ICE arrests that have reported significant declines in violent crime, including Houston, Memphis, and Nashville. But the most recent federal data do not show cause and effect, let alone a clear correlation. In New York, Philadelphia, and Los Angeles—all sanctuary cities—the murder rate is the lowest in at least a half century. [ Read: The man in charge of immigration data just resigned ] The Department of Homeland Security told us that a comparison of state-level ICE-arrest volumes and year-over-year violent-crime-count changes is improper, but did not provide evidence for the president’s own cause-and-effect claims tying the two together. “It’s common sense: when you remove illegal aliens off our streets, the violent U.S. crime rate DROPS,” DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in a statement. “President Trump is making America safe again.” The number of homicides and other violent crimes began falling in the 1990s. It spiked during the pandemic, then resumed a downward path during Joe Biden’s presidency. Elisa Jácome, an economist at Northwestern University who has studied the effects of immigration enforcement on crime, told us that although it’s easy for politicians to try to claim credit for the reduction, “it’s actually quite difficult to separate those claims from the underlying trends, which are very real.” The declining violent-crime trend is also real in countries where Trump is not president and there’s no mass-deportation campaign. Canada’s homicide rate fell 16 percent from 2024 to 2025, the biggest one-year drop in 40 years, according to a July 2026 report by the Canadian government. Homicides in England and Wales are at a nearly 50-year low, according to British government data, amid a historic influx of immigrants. T rump’s claims about crime and immigrants have been his calling card ever since he first ran for office, more than a decade ago. As his party potentially faces the loss of its congressional majority in November, he and top law-enforcement officials have been trying to fire up the MAGA faithful with the messaging that helped Republicans gain control of the House in the 2022 midterms. The president made his law-and-order pitch during a visit in August to a police academy on Long Island, where he campaigned for Bruce Blakeman, the Republican challenging New York Governor Kathy Hochul, a Democrat who is expected to easily win the race. Using rows of uniformed police officers and cadets as a backdrop, Trump mocked the state’s Democratic leaders and told the crowd the White House was full of “young, beautiful girls” who “want to be safe” while working in the nation’s capital. Republicans in tight races have been less eager to embrace Trump’s mass-deportation campaign. Representative María Elvira Salazar, a Republican whose Miami district has been roiled by immigration enforcement, released a video message last month telling Trump that ICE was picking up too many non-criminals. Other Republicans who have tried to distance themselves from the White House’s aggressive approach include Senator Roger Marshall of Kansas, where ICE has been raiding meatpacking plants. Trump won the state by 16 percentage points in 2024, but the latest polls show Marshall in a tight race with the Democratic nominee, Adam Hamilton, who says families are “living in fear” of ICE. Even longtime proponents of the president’s immigration agenda have rescinded their support. In 2017, then-Governor of Maine Paul LePage applauded Trump for signing an executive order banning immigrants from many Muslim-majority countries, saying he was in full support of Trump’s “action to protect all Americans.” But last week, LePage, who is now running for a House seat, announced at a news conference that his son’s father-in-law is being deported. Even though he came to the United States legally and has a work permit, “he came from a country that’s not the liking to certain people in Washington,” LePage said, without naming the country. “That’s not right.” [ From the November 2026 issue: The babies left behind in America ] Administration officials have claimed that upwards of 65 percent of immigrants arrested by ICE have a criminal record. But even among those with convictions or pending charges, most offenses are nonviolent, Charis Kubrin, a criminology professor at UC Irvine, told us. (In July, less than 4 percent of immigrants arrested by ICE had a past violent-crime conviction, according to an analysis by The New York Times .) In August, Kubrin released a study on changing crime rates and unauthorized-immigrant populations across nearly 12,000 U.S. neighborhoods. She found that the number of immigrants in a neighborhood is inconsequential to the amount of unlawful activity. “Increases do not cause violent crime to go up. Decreases do not cause violent crimes to go down,” she said. “It has no effect.” Those findings are consistent with dozens of other studies showing that immigrants have lower incarceration rates than native-born Americans. Trump officials have dismissed those arguments, advancing something akin to a broken-windows theory that claims permissive border policies encourage immigrants to disregard American laws. Having violated the country’s immigration rules to enter, the theory goes, they’re more inclined to commit more serious offenses once they settle into their new lives. Charles Fain Lehman, a senior fellow at the center-right Manhattan Institute, told us there’s no evidence of that. Lehman said criminal-justice scholars debate why the homicide rate has fallen so fast. They point to an array of other factors, including more powerful police surveillance and tracking tools that help cities more effectively deploy officers to areas with higher incidences of violent crime. Others posit more esoteric theories, such as the removal of lead from drinking water and fewer people consuming alcohol. Researchers generally don’t regard immigration enforcement as a significant factor, Lehman said. When immigration-enforcement officers target serious criminals, however, there are potential benefits to public safety, he said, because a small fraction of offenders commit the majority of offenses. “Some of those offenders are noncitizens who are here illegally. If you remove them from the country, then mechanically you would expect the rate of violence or of serious crime to go down,” he said. Trump has employed a version of that logic, often claiming that 2 percent of people commit 91 percent of crimes when discussing his deployment of the National Guard in Washington, D.C. (The Niskanen Center, a nonpartisan think tank, found that the National Guard had no significant impact on Washington’s decline in violent crime, but its deployment in high-visibility areas may have deterred people from committing opportunistic property offenses.) A few days after the president declared a “crime emergency” in the capital last year, Stephen Miller told reporters that “the highest degree of national-security and public-safety concern are in sanctuary cities.” Those places, Miller said, release undocumented immigrants who commit crimes back into the community, rather than turn them over to ICE. “And in many cases, those aliens will go on to commit additional serious offenses, including oftentimes—as we’ve seen over and over again—rape and murder.” FBI and census data from the past year show that neither states with sanctuary cities nor those with high immigrant populations have the highest reported incidence of sexual assault. The five states with the highest reports of rape per capita are Alaska, Arkansas, Utah, Oklahoma, and Montana. Each has a relatively low immigrant population, formalized cooperation between local law enforcement and ICE, and a Republican in the governor’s office. [ Read: An American city, with troops on its streets ] Recent polling shows that Republicans have lost their long-held advantage over Democrats on the handling of immigration, and other polls show Democrats making up ground on crime. But voters side with Republicans on those key issues more than they do on the economy or health care, and the Trump administration has been eager to highlight them, often at the same time. Attorney General Todd Blanche held an event at the Department of Justice last Thursday and promised to continue the administration’s immigration crackdown. The White House’s “border czar,” Tom Homan, who joined Blanche alongside FBI Director Kash Patel, urged criminal charges against officials running sanctuary cities. (Blanche might have difficulty finding a charge: Sanctuary policies don’t violate criminal statutes.) That afternoon, DOJ announced $25 million in grants for local law-enforcement agencies. But the eligibility requirements come with a catch: Funds are available only to jurisdictions that sign agreements to help ICE make more arrests.

items.title: The Baltic States Prepare for War
items.description: Photographs by Maciek Nabrdalik One evening this summer, in the village of Bezdonys, in eastern Lithuania, I watched as a platoon of riflemen arrived at a train station occupied by enemy forces. Some of the Lithuanians let out a burst of gunfire from across the tracks, pinning the adversary in place as the rest of the unit advanced on the station. As the firefight intensified, wounded riflemen were evacuated to makeshift medical tents. An enemy soldier lay slumped against the station’s yellow clapboard siding. Military exercises are elaborate acts of make-believe. I was observing this one to understand how a large-scale attack on the most vulnerable part of the NATO alliance might play out—and to see how the Baltic states of Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania think about their own defense. The raid in Bezdonys was part of a nationwide simulation and involved the Lithuanian Riflemen’s Union, a state-supported militia group that traces its history to the end of World War I. The Lithuanians I met wore camouflage fatigues and had no trouble accepting the scenario behind the exercise: that the enemy—Russia—had invaded their country, and that defensive forces had retreated to a city in the north. In their civilian lives, the riflemen are teachers and sales managers, economists and medical students. Now, suddenly, they were responsible for ambushing Russian outposts, killing enemy soldiers, and transmitting intelligence to the army. “The enemy has to know,” General Raimundas Vaikšnoras told me, “that if they step one foot in our territory, we will strike back.” Vaikšnoras is Lithuania’s defense chief, and his distrust of Russia, a former occupying power, is not a notional concern. Ever since Russia’s invasions of other post-Soviet nations—Georgia in 2008; Ukraine in 2014 and 2022— conflict with Moscow has been front of mind for the people of the Baltic states. The three countries are small—Lithuania, the largest, is about the size of West Virginia—and grouped, one atop the other, on the shores of the Baltic Sea. They are also linked geopolitically by their common experience on Russia’s western borderlands, one of subjugation and dispossession. The Baltic states escaped some of that past after the fall of communism and the breakup of the Soviet Union, when they regained their sovereignty. And they took measures to solidify that status when they joined NATO, in 2004, attaching themselves to the American-led security order. They have much to lose from what looks to be the unraveling of that order. Donald Trump has mused repeatedly about taking the United States out of NATO. On the campaign trail in 2024, he encouraged the Russians to do “whatever the hell they want” to NATO members delinquent in their defense spending. This year, he threatened to invade Greenland , a self-governing territory of Denmark, an alliance member. When European partners declined to join his war of choice against Iran, he disparaged NATO as a “paper tiger.” [ Read: Europe without America ] Even a small incursion by Russia into the Baltics could be catastrophic if NATO did not adequately respond, thereby breaking the promise of collective defense enshrined in Article 5 of the founding treaty—an attack on one is an attack on all. Over breakfast in Washington, D.C., earlier this year, I asked Jens Stoltenberg, a former NATO secretary-general, whether he was confident that Trump would help defend the Baltic states in the event of a Russian attack. He said, “We base our security on that,” a careful reply that stated an incontrovertible fact but did not answer the question. © OpenMapTiles; © OpenStreetMap The threat of Russian expansionism may feel remote in the United States. But the idea that Russian soldiers might invade their countries doesn’t seem implausible to the 6 million people who live in the Baltic states. It has happened before. The Second World War brought Soviet and Nazi invasions, and the postwar Soviet occupation threatened to extinguish Lithuania entirely. (“Lithuania is beautiful without the Lithuanians,” a Politburo member once remarked.) In 1990, Lithuania became the first Soviet republic to declare its independence, and since then has transformed itself into a lively democracy with a high-tech economy. But it remains uniquely vulnerable: hemmed in to the east by the Russian satellite state of Belarus and to the west by the sea, and pinched to the south by the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, home to Russia’s Baltic Fleet and a staging ground for ballistic missiles capable of reaching most of Europe. Nuclear weapons are likely stored there too. Lithuania spends more on defense as a share of its economic output than any other NATO country, and for years has urged the West to take Russian aggression more seriously. The possibility of war is lodged in its politics, its economy, and its psyche; the memory of occupation haunts its present and its view of the future. [ Read: Europeans have realized their error ] Whether Russia has imminent designs on the independent Baltic countries it once ruled is a matter of dispute, though the dispute centers mainly on the word imminent , not on Moscow’s desires. The Russian military is in poor condition in key respects. The cost of recruiting is high, armor stocks are dwindling, and corruption is endemic . But Russia has improved its performance in other areas, including its use of drones and glide bombs, and its agile infantry tactics. A recent American-led air exercise in Poland and the Baltic states, which massed fighter aircraft near Kaliningrad, seemed designed to warn Moscow of the costs of adventurism. Many analysts believe that any mobilization against the Baltics would come only after the end of hostilities in Ukraine, where almost all capable Russian ground forces are currently engaged. Ukraine, Vaikšnoras noted hopefully, is “keeping Russians away.” Others see Russian President Vladimir Putin’s incentives differently, fearing that he might wish to act sooner, exploiting the interval in which the U.S. commitment to Europe seems to be faltering but Europe’s rearmament, after decades of disinvestment, is incomplete. Russian coordination with China—timing an attack in Europe to coincide with a move by Beijing against Taiwan—could be disastrous. Some U.S. and European officials I spoke with believe that the high burn rate of American munitions in Iran may increase Russia’s appetite to test NATO with a limited ground attack in the Baltics. The aim would be a fait accompli, taking a small piece of territory so quickly that the defenders decide the cost of reversal is too high. Putin once boasted that Russian forces could seize the Baltic capitals in two days. A Putin ally not long ago described Latvia, Lithuania’s neighbor to the north, as a “nonexistent country.” Maciek Nabrdalik for The Atlantic General Raimundas Vaikšnoras, Lithuania’s chief of defense, at his office in Vilnius For the Baltic nations, “wait and see” is not a strategy. Distrust of Russian intentions has given rise to a low-grade but pervasive dread that hangs over daily life and has an impact on all institutions. Cities constantly hone their evacuation plans. Hospitals can shift at once to a wartime footing. After Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine, membership in the Lithuanian Riflemen’s Union doubled, and now stands at about 20,000. When I visited Vaikšnoras, he brought me to an alcove behind his office where his helmet, rucksack, and body armor were hanging on a small wooden stand. It’s his job to imagine the worst. But as I learned during a month spent talking with political and military leaders, it’s also true that, in a struggle for survival, the Baltic states possess advantages. They are ready to commit their whole societies to the fight. What they no longer know is whether the United States will be by their side—and in Russian eyes, uncertainty may seem like an invitation. THE FIRST DAY What would a Russian attack on the Baltic states look like? It could come in the form of outright invasion, designed to control all three countries and restore what Russia has declared to be its rightful sphere of influence. It could come in the form of “hybrid war,” which the Baltic states have gotten a taste of already: think cyberintrusions, assassination attempts, arson, damage to undersea infrastructure, interference with GPS frequencies, and a deliberately heightened volume of asylum flows—transporting desperate migrants from the Middle East and Africa to the border of European Union countries, as Belarus has done since 2021. Russia could also stir up unrest among the Russian-speaking minority who still live in the Baltic states—a scenario that figures in If Russia Wins , a best-selling book published last year by the academic analyst Carlo Masala. Short of invading all three countries, Russia could attempt to close the Suwałki Gap—the small patch of border that Lithuania shares with Poland, stretching for roughly 40 miles between Kaliningrad and Belarus. This corridor is the only friendly overland route between the Baltic states and the rest of NATO Europe—an essential lifeline. [ Read: Russia’s hybrid-war strategy in Europe ] Despite the shortcomings revealed by its war in Ukraine, Russia would be a formidable adversary. It is willing to send soldiers to their deaths by the hundreds of thousands, and it possesses nuclear weapons. Baltic leaders do not make the mistake of thinking that Russia will behave the way they want it to. As former U.S. Defense Secretary James Mattis has cautioned, about all military conflict, “The enemy gets a vote.” That said, it would be hard to hide large-scale Russian preparations for invasion. Baltic intelligence officers are so focused on every permutation of the Russian threat that their mindset was summarized to me this way by a European expert in Baltic security: “If a seagull shits in the harbor, we know what it had for breakfast, we know where it nests, and we know when it last went to Russia.” When I visited Vaikšnoras, I noticed on his desk a map of a new training area, planned for the southwestern part of the country, right near the Suwałki Gap. If enemy troops start massing on Russian or Belarusian territory, Lithuanian troops will assemble opposite them—force-shadowing, as it is called. The Baltic states can’t trade space for time—a classic defensive strategy that involves yielding territory in order to exhaust the enemy, then waiting until a counterattack becomes feasible. Vilnius, the capital, home to 600,000 people, is a mere 20 miles from Belarus. In the early days of an invasion, it would quickly be threatened by the Russian army. The Baltic states need to hold off the invaders for as long as possible, hoping that allied help will arrive—whether in the form of ground forces or, even more useful, airpower—before the situation becomes irretrievable. Lithuania’s military, though the largest among the Baltic states, is nonetheless modest: some 60,000 men and women in active and reserve units. In an emergency, and with the assistance of well-trained volunteer groups such as the Riflemen, the number could swell to more than 80,000—still small compared with any potential Russian force. To help contain the enemy forces and keep them as close to the border as possible, the Baltic states are building a defensive line—digging anti-tank ditches and erecting concrete obstacles called “dragon’s teeth” because of their hulking triangular shape. Maciek Nabrdalik for The Atlantic Anti-tank “dragon’s teeth” on Lithuania’s heavily fortified border with Belarus Modern technology could make a big difference. The plan is to saturate the border with infrared cameras and acoustic sensors, a network modeled on a Ukrainian system called Sky Fortress. Data gathered by this equipment would be shared with allies and analyzed by artificial intelligence to help determine the best way to neutralize incoming threats. Border areas could also be heavily mined. All three Baltic states, along with Poland and Finland, have withdrawn from the 1997 Ottawa Treaty, aimed at eliminating antipersonnel land mines, which can kill or maim civilians long after conflicts have ended. The move caused some disquiet in allied capitals. The reply from the Baltics was, What choice do we have? One afternoon, two soldiers picked me up outside the ministry of defense in a military off-roader, and we drove east to the Belarusian border. The terrain is flat, seemingly favorable to an attacker. But it’s also full of spongy bogs, which serve as natural choke points. Last year, four American soldiers died during a training mission in Lithuania when their 70-ton armored truck sank in a wetland. Lithuania is re-creating swamps and reforesting parts of the border to force the enemy into predictable routes. Man-made obstacles are layered on top of natural barriers to channel (or, in military parlance, canalize) the enemy into narrow zones. The dragon’s teeth rise to about chest height, and they’re linked by a tangle of metal cords. The fortifications are perhaps the most conspicuous part of Baltic war planning. Rather than destroying a tank outright, the dragon’s teeth catch a vehicle’s underside, where its armor is thinner, and lift the hull off the ground. This leaves the vehicle stranded and vulnerable to artillery and anti-tank missiles. The military has bottleneck coordinates already plotted, anticipating that the enemy will need to slow at specific points. A breach attempt at a fortified point would create extraordinary violence: tanks caught on dragon’s teeth, mines detonating, artillery landing on the stalled convoy, drones circling overhead to hit anything left moving. Meanwhile, the Baltic states would be striking deep in enemy territory. All three Baltic countries have ordered missile launchers called HIMARS, and their most powerful precision-strike missiles have a range of about 190 miles. That’s almost exactly the distance from Tallinn, the capital of Estonia, to the Russian city of St. Petersburg. THE FIRST 72 HOURS Given the likely warning signs, political and military consultations would begin within NATO before Russian troops cross any border. When the Baltic states joined the alliance, NATO leaders initially resisted developing plans for their defense so as not to provoke conflict with the Kremlin. Then, in 2008, Russia invaded Georgia. That year, a senior Russian official and close associate of Putin’s publicly described the Baltic states, along with Crimea and other parts of Ukraine, as “traditional territory of the Russian nation.” In response, an existing NATO playbook for the defense of Poland was extended to the Baltics. But only meager forces were pre-positioned, and reinforcement timelines were inexact. Implicitly, the strategy was to cede territory in hopes of later taking it back. Widespread Russian atrocities in Ukraine following the 2022 invasion made that prospect unacceptable, and Baltic leaders pressed for changes. A year later, the alliance adopted new regional defense plans aimed at containing and countering an incursion, rather than rolling it back. The main conference chamber at NATO headquarters, in Brussels, is known as Room 1—an amphitheater with an oval table in the middle. This is where ambassadors would gather in the event of an attack to consider a bid by the Baltic states for a declaration under Article 5—the necessary first step toward a collective response. The ambassadors make up the North Atlantic Council, the alliance’s main political decision-making body. They would seek options from NATO’s military committee, composed of the member states’ national-defense representatives. Remigijus Baltrėnas, a Lithuanian general, currently leads NATO’s military staff, although NATO doesn’t have any forces of its own; everything is provided by member countries. When I asked Baltrėnas if he believed that the alliance would come to the aid of the Baltic states, he said, “I’m convinced, practically, that if it will be needed, nations will be able to push aside their national ambitions, their national restrictions, and agree for the cohesion and defense of the alliance, to move forward with whatever is necessary.” But as the clauses and qualifications in his gnarly statement suggest, it would be, as he put it, a “painful process.” Different alliance members will view the risk of escalation differently. Some may even have different interpretations of the facts. A new color-coded alert system dictates what degree of mobilization is called for: yellow, amber, and red, with the last meaning that an attack is imminent or has already started. The Supreme Allied Commander Europe, who leads all NATO military operations, has the authority to rush certain forces to the region before the member countries reach a consensus. An American has held that job since the alliance’s founding, in 1949. Today, it belongs to Alexus G. Grynkewich, an Air Force general. He can call upon tens of thousands of troops supplied by member countries; their duty is to be mission-ready and able to deploy within 10 days of activation. Maciek Nabrdalik for The Atlantic Members of the Lithuanian Riflemen’s Union monitor military exercises from a facility in Vilnius. The U.S. military has been training Lithuanian troops and other armed forces in the Baltics for years. The Riflemen’s exercise I witnessed in Lithuania took place at the conclusion of a nine-week commando course run by the 1st Battalion of the Army’s 12th Cavalry Regiment, deployed from Fort Hood, Texas. But the American battalion was rotating out of the country the next day—and there would be no “heel to toe” replacement, as there had been since 2019. That may seem like a small thing, but it occasions nervousness about a larger one. Deterrence is about signaling, and the Baltic nations need Russia to believe that Washington would treat an attack on their territory as an attack on all NATO members. In the past, the U.S. has spoken loudly in support of the Baltic countries. On a trip to Vilnius in 2002, President George W. Bush vowed that “anyone who would choose Lithuania as an enemy has also made an enemy of the United States of America.” Those words are engraved on a plaque outside the entrance of city hall. Do they remain true more than two decades later? NATO could be drawn into a conflict regardless. Each of the Baltic states hosts allied forces, initially assembled in the years after Russia’s annexation of Crimea in 2014 and then expanded after the invasion in 2022. Multinational forces were originally intended as trip wires that would compel a larger NATO force to intervene. Now their mission is contributing to a credible defense from the very start of an invasion. Kris Reeves, a Canadian colonel who until recently commanded multinational forces in Latvia, told me, “I can fight tonight and tell Ottawa tomorrow.” The brigade in Lithuania is expanding to include 5,000 Germans and the latest tanks for added firepower and mobility. About 20 countries contribute to military forces in the three Baltic states, led by Germany, Canada, and Britain. Žilvinas Gaubys, a brigadier general who heads Lithuania’s training-and-doctrine command, told me that the military has considered a scenario in which help from Washington is delayed or does not arrive—indeed, war games have been conducted that consider this premise. Military planners, the general said, must test “the most difficult scenarios.” According to established war plans, American forces stationed in Poland or Germany should be activated from the “first minute” of an invasion, Gaubys explained. But what happens if that minute goes by and the Americans don’t come? The presence of other international forces offers a measure of reassurance. So, too, according to Baltic officials, does the progress made by NATO’s European members in acquiring certain capabilities, such as aerial refueling, that the U.S. once mostly provided. But there would be no easy replacement for American satellite intelligence, or for American missiles and hypersonics capable of reaching far behind the front line. Loss of American support would diminish what the Baltic states can see and what they can strike. NATO planners know that, early on, Russia would rely not only on physical force but also on cyberwarfare to disable critical infrastructure in the Baltic states—the energy, transport, water, and communications systems that enable their societies to function. The vulnerability, however, goes both ways. When it comes to cyberoperations, Estonia is a global leader. It made cybercapabilities a priority after a sweeping digital assault brought down government and commercial servers in 2007—a surprise move by Russia or Russian sympathizers to protest the relocation of a Soviet-era statue. In response, Estonia established a dedicated cybercommand within its armed forces, as well as a cyberunit within the Estonian Defence League, a volunteer reserve team drawing on the country’s immense civilian IT talent pool. One way reservists contribute is by looking inside successful Ukrainian technology—the Baltic states understand how Ukraine’s innovations are transforming the nature of warfare. [ Read: Lessons from the world’s most tech-savvy government ] Estonia’s cybercommand is led by a taciturn colonel named René Innos. When I met him over the summer, in Tallinn, he was wearing combat fatigues and black boots but had the tired and under-exercised look of someone who spends most of his time looking at a computer screen. Part of his job, he said, is defensive: Every year, he sees billions of “knocks on the door” by Russian hackers looking to penetrate Estonian networks. But the cybercommand is capable of offensive operations too, and it would be an invisible but major part of any war. One objective, Innos said, would be to disrupt the “kill chain”—the communications links that connect target acquisition and target destruction. Another objective would be simply sowing confusion. The enemy, of course, is renowned for its own digital expertise. Both sides would be asking, What is the next new trick? THE FIRST WEEK The conflict would soon begin to stabilize—not to ease, necessarily, but to unfold along more predictable lines. Both sides would be using a dense network of drones, sensors, and mines, making a surprise breakthrough on the front difficult to achieve. Russian infantry and armored vehicles would be detected by drone reconnaissance and then destroyed before they could generate momentum and push past defensive fortifications. Many of the defenders wouldn’t be firing machine guns or driving tanks. They’d be operating small quadcopters known as FPV drones, because of the first-person view they give remote pilots. FPV drones mostly function as one-way strike weapons, though the same airframes can fly reconnaissance. One Lithuanian colonel estimates that 80 to 90 percent of Russian casualties could be inflicted by FPV drones. A visit to a training area in the southwestern part of Lithuania, about 30 miles from the border with Kaliningrad, gave me a sense of the country’s growing drone capabilities. Trainees were sitting behind a pair of laptops placed on a folding table in a tent. A Monster Energy drink was open on the table. The primary pilot used simple mouse clicks to direct an airborne vehicle—an Estonian-made reconnaissance drone with a range of about 30 miles. Sitting alongside, his co-pilot operated the camera system using a joystick resembling a PlayStation controller. I had come to the training area from Kaunas, Lithuania’s second-largest city, where a military-drone laboratory occupies space in a glass-sheathed university building. The army is using the facility to turn soldiers into engineers. FPV drones are cheap—they can cost only a few hundred dollars apiece—but also full of bugs. Being able to replace a battery in the field could save money and lives. Inside the lab, an airy space with soldering irons and fume extractors, soldiers in army fatigues were bent over worktables. A reservist in jeans and a T-shirt stood at a whiteboard, delivering a lesson about the battery’s power connector and protective casing. Nearby, university students were completing an academic 3-D-printing project, unconnected with warfare. They appeared unbothered by the military preparations, which are difficult to keep neatly apart from civilian life. Schools operated by the ministry of defense are teaching children as young as 10 how to assemble, program, and fly drones. Paula Bronstein / Getty A trainee learns to fly an attack drone at a military school near Lviv, in Ukraine. I was in the company of Arnoldas Sadauskas, a major in the Lithuanian armed forces. Earlier, I had seen in the back of his van a pile of torpedo-shaped warheads with propellers, which he showed me while casually lighting a cigarette. The most important lesson to learn, Sadauskas said, is the need for improvisation. He brought up Ukraine, as Baltic commanders often do. Its armed forces no longer wait for foreign companies to provide state-of-the-art equipment. Ukraine builds its own, and constantly changes the technical composition to elude electronic countermeasures. The takeaway—that technical advances can make up for a relative disadvantage in troop strength—is now dogma in Baltic defense thinking. Officers from Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania make frequent trips to Ukraine. I asked Sadauskas if he was adapting lessons from Americans too. He said, “I don’t know what they have to teach me.” In a sustained conflict, the Baltic states would need private industry to replenish weapons stocks and modify technology as battlefield dynamics change. Because of their size, the Baltic states don’t build heavy platforms, such as battle tanks and self-propelled artillery. Their advantage lies in niche areas, including electronics, optics, and ammunition components. The field of photonics, devoted to generating and controlling light, is especially strong in Vilnius. Julius Skruibis, the chief technology officer of Aktyvus Photonics, told me that the city is home to no fewer than 60 companies active in this area. Aktyvus Photonics is in a tech hub on the outskirts of Vilnius, and I met Skruibis at the company’s offices. He gave me a pair of sunglasses, and with our eyes shielded and shoes wrapped in plastic coverings, we entered an antiseptic space where engineers in blue lab coats were experimenting with laser designators—highly concentrated light sources used to “light up” military targets. These laser beams guide munitions to their destinations. The company has developed a handheld designator for the Ukrainian armed forces. In my hand, it felt like a state-of-the-art film camera, smooth and compact. The designator has a range of six miles. The drawback is that a soldier using one from a ground position, kneeling and pointing it at a target, risks exposure to the enemy. The company’s newest designator, not much bigger than a Duracell nine-volt battery, can be lifted by a small drone, and is now the biggest-selling Aktyvus product. Keeping the designator steady is the challenge; it’s buffeted both by wind and by vibrations from the drone. Digital stabilization is able to remove imperfections in the video feed, but there’s as yet no analogue for adjusting the beam of light. The company is working intensively on stabilization technology to hold the designator in place. Skruibis was frank about the kind of accuracy he’s seeking: He placed an index finger on his forehead, right between his eyes. THE FIRST MONTH The consequences of any conflict in the Baltic states will quickly expand outward. Within a month of the war launched by the U.S. and Israel against Iran in February, it had grown to involve more than a dozen other countries , closed the Strait of Hormuz, and sent global oil prices to their highest levels in years. Some ramifications of a Baltic conflict are unpredictable, but one is not: The Baltic Sea would become a contested strategic space. One of the keys to controlling the Baltic Sea is Gotland, a Swedish island about 80 miles from the Baltic states. Its sandy beaches and limestone cliffs make it a tourist jewel. It is also vital to establishing air and naval dominance over the entire region. Several years ago, Russian state television hosted a reserve officer and pro-Kremlin commentator who explained how Russian forces could commandeer Gotland, which is about the size of Long Island, and leverage it as a base while Moscow set about conquering the Baltic states. Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania have no combat aircraft of their own, and only gunboat navies. Lithuania’s largest ship is a minelayer that came used from Norway. Maciek Nabrdalik for The Atlantic A sign reading #MesNATO, or “We Are NATO” in Lithuanian, outside the defense ministry’s headquarters, in Vilnius Sweden and Finland joined NATO in the aftermath of Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine, casting aside a long tradition of neutrality and military nonalignment. One day this summer, I met Sweden’s defense chief, Michael Claesson, on the deck of the Carlskrona, which at 350 feet has the distinction of being the longest ship in the Swedish navy. It packs little firepower but bristles with masts, antennas, radar arrays, and communications equipment. It was docked in the harbor at Visby, Gotland’s capital. The fortification of Gotland, Claesson explained, would allow NATO to project air and maritime superiority in the broader Baltic Sea region. Kaliningrad is to the southeast. Rockets and long-range missiles launched from Gotland could easily strike Russian supply lines and other infrastructure supporting military operations in the Baltics. The island is an ideal staging ground for fighter jets: close enough to high-value Russian targets but far enough away to be untouchable by short-range drones launched from Russian terrain. That enviable location has earned the island its description as an “unsinkable aircraft carrier.” Hostilities would convulse the entire maritime zone, one of the busiest in the world for commerce. Trade and civilian traffic in the Baltic would be suspended, with priority given to reinforcement and evacuation efforts. Moscow is not without options, even if the Baltic Sea, ringed almost entirely by Western allies, has come to be seen as a “NATO lake.” Russia still has access to Baltic waters from ports at St. Petersburg and Kaliningrad. It could provide military escorts for its merchant fleet and target undersea cables used for power and communication. Missiles from Kaliningrad could menace maritime operations and hold regional economies hostage. In some ways, Gotland is to NATO what Kaliningrad is to Russia—a forward outpost that helps control access to a vital theater of operations. Which is why the island itself is vulnerable to attack, and why war could spread quickly to Sweden. The Swedish armed forces disbanded the island’s last defensive regiment in 2005 and began restoring its defenses only after Russia’s annexation of Crimea. In 2022, as Russian troops massed on Ukraine’s border, Sweden dispatched additional units to Gotland. Armored vehicles clambered down Visby’s medieval streets. The government in Stockholm is building new barracks and other facilities, and Sweden’s military has conducted joint exercises involving U.S. Marines. Bolstering the garrison on Gotland remains a work in progress, and a visitor may well be more aware of archaeological activity (the island has been settled, sparsely, for millennia) than of a humming military presence. Ewa Skoog Haslum, a vice admiral and Sweden’s chief of joint operations, was blunt about her view when we spoke: “We have too few forces on Gotland.” Moscow is definitely aware of Gotland’s strategic value. Russia’s ambassador to Sweden recently accused the government in Stockholm of “provocative steps” on Gotland, vowing that Moscow would “take all of this into account in our military-political planning.” Maciek Nabrdalik for The Atlantic General Michael Claesson, Sweden’s defense chief, aboard the Carlskrona in Gotland Although NATO forces have trained on Gotland, offensive weapons aren’t currently stored there. I asked Claesson how long it would take to turn Gotland into a platform for serious offensive operations. “Days,” he said, holding up a few fingers. “Days on one hand.” ENDGAME Men in hooded suits, gas masks, and orange boots lifted bodies from wheeled gurneys and placed them on folding tables: yet another training exercise, this one taking place in a barracks belonging to the Vitkus Engineer Battalion, in Kaunas. The battalion builds defensive fortifications, clears land mines, and removes chemical and biological hazards. The premise of the training exercise was that the enemy had used chemical weapons against civilians. Victims had to be cut out of their clothes and doused with soapy water. Medics triaged cases while a decontamination team rushed people through washing stations. The equipment came from the Defense Threat Reduction Agency, the part of the U.S. Department of Defense responsible for countering weapons of mass destruction. The longer a war persists, and the deeper into civilian society it penetrates, the more resources the engineer battalion will require. Its commander told me that its motto is “First in, last out.” The battalion is still finding and disposing of mines and other unexploded ordnance from both world wars. It is named for Juozas Vitkus, a colonel in the country’s interwar army who helped train members of the Lithuanian Riflemen’s Union. He was killed by Soviet troops in 1946. The Lithuanians I met in military barracks, on training fields, and at government offices all wanted to make sure I witnessed the many ways in which the United States is still participating in their defense—presumably, they want to believe, with every intention of assisting in a potential war with Russia. Strategic culture in the Baltics is indebted to American guidance. Many generals have studied and trained in the United States. When I met with Vaikšnoras, the Lithuanian defense chief, I noticed a photograph of his graduating class at the U.S. Army War College, where he received a master’s degree in 2013. Ties between the two militaries remain close. And although many nations, including NATO allies, are skittish about having nuclear weapons based on their soil, Lithuania is revising its constitution to permit such staging . But the American commitment to NATO—to countries such as Poland and Germany, never mind the Baltic states—is no longer a given . As I watched U.S. Army personnel give pointers to Lithuanian troops, I wondered if they might be among the last American military representatives engaged in Europe in this way. Maciek Nabrdalik for The Atlantic During military exercises, Lithuanian Riflemen’s Union volunteers clear a railway station in the town of Bezdonys. These days, the truly inescapable sight in Lithuania is not the Stars and Stripes but the blue-and-yellow flag of Ukraine. It flies outside government ministries. It is draped inside hipster coffee shops. Near the Neris River, which cuts through the capital, I saw a bird feeder painted in blue and yellow. Don’t mistake this for a mere token of solidarity. It is a badge acknowledging Ukraine’s contribution to the defense of Europe. The Baltics are sometimes described as the Cassandra of European states—doomed for their prescience. But the metaphor is not quite right. Vilnius isn’t Troy, and it wasn’t sacked when Lithuania’s warnings about Russian expansionism were vindicated in 2022. For now, Ukraine is absorbing the Russian onslaught, and giving survival lessons to other vulnerable democracies. One counterpoint to a weakening American military presence in Europe has been an acceleration of visits by European military leaders to Ukraine. My interview with General Gaubys had to be cut short because he was scheduled for a trip to the Ukrainian battlefield. Questions about the future of the American-led order are unavoidable in Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania. The doubts provoked by Trump about the principle of collective defense will not easily be assuaged or argued away. But I also encountered something else: the emergence of a new order, in which Ukraine matters as much to the security of Europe as the United States does. Baltic soldiers are in Ukraine every day, embedding with officers close to the front line, helping where they can, but most of all learning, adopting their tactics, and preparing their own defense. They believe that war with Russia is coming. They would prefer to have American backing when it does. But they’ll fight without the United States if they need to. This article appears in the November 2026 print edition with the headline “The Next Front.”

items.title: Algérie-Russie : Alger veut attirer davantage d’investissements russes
items.description: Une nouvelle etape dans le renforcement du partenariat economique entre l'Algerie et la Russie a ete engagee le 29 septembre a l'occasion d'une reunion a distance entre le directeur general de l'Agence algerienne de promotion de l'investissement (AAPI), Omar Rekkache, et le president du Conseil d'affaires algero-russe, Ahmed Azimov. La rencontre, a laquelle a egalement participe l'ambassadeur d'Algerie en Russie, Toufik Djouamaa, s'inscrit dans le prolongement des conclusions de la 13ᵉ session de la Commission mixte algero-russe, tenue a Moscou du 24 au 26 juin dernier, selon un communique de l'AAPI. Les discussions ont notamment porte sur l'elaboration d'un programme d'action commun visant a mieux faire connaître les opportunites d'investissement disponibles en Algerie aupres des operateurs economiques russes. Les deux parties souhaitent egalement intensifier les echanges entre l'AAPI et le monde des affaires afin de favoriser la creation de partenariats et la realisation de projets a forte valeur ajoutee. Une « Journee de l'Algerie » a Moscou La preparation d'une « Journee de l'Algerie » a egalement ete abordee. Cette manifestation devrait etre organisee en marge du Sommet et du Forum economique Russie-Afrique, prevus a Moscou a la fin du mois d'octobre. Elle doit servir de plateforme pour presenter aux investisseurs russes les potentialites de l'economie algerienne ainsi que les opportunites offertes par son marche. L'objectif est notamment de faciliter les contacts directs entre les operateurs des deux pays et de faire emerger de nouveaux projets d'investissement. Lors de la reunion, Omar Rekkache a presente plusieurs secteurs consideres comme susceptibles d'interesser les investisseurs russes. Il a notamment cite l'agriculture, l'energie et les energies renouvelables, l'industrie et les industries de transformation, ainsi que l'industrie pharmaceutique et les dispositifs medicaux. Le responsable de l'AAPI a egalement reaffirme la disponibilite de l'agence a accompagner les investisseurs et a faciliter la concretisation de leurs projets en Algerie. Technologies et expertise De son cote, Ahmed Azimov a fait etat de l'interet manifeste par des entreprises russes pour le marche algerien. Il a particulierement insiste sur l'importance du transfert de technologies et du partage de connaissances dans le developpement de futurs partenariats. Par ailleurs, le president du Conseil d'affaires algero-russe a assure que son organisation etait disposee a contribuer a la promotion des opportunites d'investissement en Algerie et a renforcer la mise en relation entre les entreprises russes et algeriennes. Cette volonte de renforcer les investissements s'inscrit ainsi dans une dynamique plus large de consolidation des relations economiques entre Alger et Moscou, l'accent etant mis sur les partenariats industriels, le transfert de savoir-faire et la realisation de projets dans des secteurs juges prioritaires.

items.title: Consumer inflation eases to 10.3pc in September from 11.1pc in August, official data shows
items.description: ISLAMABAD: Consumer inflation eased to 10.3 per cent in September from 11.1pc a month earlier, mainly due to a sharp slowdown in food inflation, the Pakistan Bureau of Statistics said on Thursday. The slight deceleration in the inflation rate, measured by the Consumer Price Index, reversed the sharp increase recorded in August, when higher food and energy prices pushed the annual rate to 11.1pc from 9.2pc in July. The easing was more pronounced in rural areas, where inflation fell to 10.5pc from 12.2pc, while urban inflation edged down to 10.1pc from 10.4pc. The September reading was also within the Ministry of Finance’s projection of 10pc to 11pc for the month in its Monthly Economic Update and Outlook for September 2026. However, despite the decline in the annual rate, prices rose 1.3pc month-on-month in September. The annual inflation rate was 5.8pc in September last year. The easing was largely driven by food prices. Food inflation dropped to 8.1pc in urban areas in September from 12.1pc in August. The decline was much sharper in rural areas, where food inflation fell to 7.7pc from 13.2pc a month earlier. However, non-food inflation moved in the opposite direction, indicating continued pressure on household expenses. Urban non-food inflation accelerated to 11.5pc from 9.4pc in August, while rural non-food inflation increased to 13.1pc from 11.3pc. The finance ministry had warned in its September 2026 outlook that inflationary pressures were concentrated in food and energy following the impact of higher global oil prices on domestic energy, transport and food costs. In August, food, housing and utilities, and transport together contributed 8.2 percentage points, or about three-quarters of headline inflation. Food alone contributed 4.9 percentage points. The latest data show that the composition of inflation shifted in September. While food inflation slowed sharply, electricity and transport costs continued to rise. Electricity charges increased by 15.28pc from the previous month, while motor fuel prices rose by 10.76pc in urban areas. At the national level, transport costs increased by 5.75pc during September and were 27.43pc higher than in the same month last year. Housing, water, electricity, gas and fuels increased by 3.05pc during the month and by 12.39pc on an annual basis. Core inflation, which excludes volatile food and energy components, also eased slightly. It stood at 8.6pc in urban areas in September, compared with 8.8pc in August, while the rural rate declined to 8.1pc from 8.5pc.
