And then also, even if you don’t feel that, everybody you care about is like that. So you can’t help but feel this way. Rosin: Yeah. I mean, I lived in just, like, a mixed immigrant neighborhood. And it sounds like you lived in a—no, you didn’t live in a Korean neighborhood. Lee: There’s so many. Like, I didn’t know white people existed. Rosin: You did not? Lee: No. You know why? Because nobody was white. You were from Pakistan. You were from India. You were from all these different countries, so you always had a country affiliation. So even if you were white you would say, I’m Polish . Rosin: Yeah. Lee: I’m Italian . I’m Irish . Rosin: Yes. Lee: And if you spoke Spanish, whatever country you came from, they’re like, Oh, he’s Spanish, and you’re like—and then you don’t think about the country, you think like, Oh, no, actually he’s from Ecuador . Rosin: Right. Lee: But then if you’re from, let’s say, the Dominican Republic, you’re like, “Oh, no, I am not Puerto Rican.” Rosin: Yes. Yes. That was actually the big battle in my middle school, was between Dominicans and Puerto Ricans. Lee: Yeah, DR, PR. Rosin: And the big thing was lunch. That’s what I remember. Like, it was What language you speak? and What did you bring to school for lunch? That’s where all the divides came in. Anyway, okay, to your novel. I did an informal survey of friends, and I would say less than half of them knew what the word hagwon meant, nor did they understand the whole culture of hagwon and what comes along with that word, so I think we need to start there. What is it? Lee: So a hagwon is a learning center. Anytime you pay somebody to teach you something that’s not in regular school, that’s a hagwon. So in Korea, everybody goes to hagwons. The elderly, the child, the middle-aged person goes to hagwon to learn gourmet cooking, tap dancing, singing. Rosin: But this makes it sound lovely, like a hagwon. Lee: No, it is actually lovely. Because you have the optionality of self-improvement, and that’s very normal. And then you also have hagwons for civil-service exams, as well as when you’re 4 years old, you go to hagwon to learn English. So that’s the hagwon that people are really—I think Americans get really upset about. Rosin: Ah. And I know you did a lot of research into hagwons. Can you just talk about the range? Like, was there a memory as you were looking into hagwons where you thought, Oh, this is very stressful , and other times when you thought, Oh, this is lovely? Lee: Oh. I think before I started the research, I thought it was very stressful because I read all the data, and the data is terrifying. So, like,, 80 percent of Koreans send their 5-year-olds to hagwon. So as a Western person, as an immigrant, as an American, you’re kinda going, “That’s kind of a lot.” Rosin: Yeah. Lee: And also, you learn that the middle income of a Korean person was, let’s say, $35,000, and you’re spending $400 a month to hagwon bills for your 4-year-old, which apparently explains the low birth rate and the low marriage rate of Korea. So I found that really stressful. And then, of course, I go to all the different hagwons, and I don’t feel stressful at all. Rosin: Oh, interesting. Lee: Because they’re so normal. And then even the hagwons in America, I thought they’re actually necessary. Rosin: Interesting. Lee: I did a complete 180. Rosin: Really? So you started out with the stereotype of hagwons— Lee: Yes, based on the data. Rosin: —like this is torturing children. They are— Lee: Don’t get a childhood. Rosin: They don’t get a childhood. They’re not able to play. Lee: All of it. Rosin: They’re being crammed with information. And that is not what you came out thinking? Lee: I do not believe that anymore. Rosin: Interesting. Lee: I don’t think that they’re lovely, but I see why they’re necessary. Rosin: Even if it means that children. I mean, my stereotype, and I’ve visited Korea, so I know a little bit, is that it’s the number of hours, it’s the quantity of hours you are expected to spend in school. Lee: Yeah. And I think that if you’re a working parent and you have kids, hagwons are a kind of child care. And also, because you can’t help the kids with homework, so then parents will actually outsource this, and it becomes a low-cost way to get tutoring. So if you think about it that way, all of a sudden, every working parent in America is like maybe, Why don’t I do that? Rosin: Yeah. It’s like high-end aftercare. Yeah. It’s— Lee: —all very good. Well, it’s kinda like Kumon. Rosin: Yeah. Lee: Kumon is very inexpensive in America. And if your kid does Kumon, then you could be a legal secretary or somebody’s assistant-chief-of-staff kind of person and say, “You know, that’s $400 a month. I make $80,000 a year, and my kid can do these worksheets, get the stickers and the stuffed animals, and the kid will be probably in the top 10 percent of my public school.” Rosin: Okay. So in the novel, there’s a mixed portrait. So for example, there’s a character named Ginny. And she’s almost a Dickensian character. She feels the most Dickensian of your characters. She’s sort of an urchin. You know, she’s sent by her parents at 9 years old to the U.S. Her sole mission is to get into UCSF and go to medical school and be a doctor, but that means she ends up at a boarding house. Where does this child come from, and what does she represent? Lee: They’re all around us, these kids. So sociologists call them “parachute children.” And they usually come from East Asia, and they’re parachuted down to another country, not necessarily always America—’cause America’s actually quite expensive—and the person who takes care of them is called the “homestay person,” the guardian. And you can pay somebody that you know or a family member, and you pay room and board. However, if you don’t have the money to pay, where does this child go? Rosin: So you just said that to me pretty neutrally, as if there’s no heartbreak involved in the story of Ginny. Is that actually how you feel or interpret Ginny? Lee: No. What I really think is interesting to me is that the people who do it think of it as an extraordinary privilege to get to do it. It’s not like you’re trying to get rid of your kid. You’re thinking, I will scrape and save and borrow to send my kid overseas, because we think the American education is that important because my kid has to be a global child . Rosin: And do you see it that way? Lee: No. But you know what I do think? I think that what we don’t think about in America is the global contextualization of these parents’ decisions. We’re talking about people who have nothing, or very close to nothing, and they’re trying to figure out, How do I become an elite person? Not me, but my child become an elite person. Like, how do I give my kid a shot? And it’s usually through exams. So you’ll have somebody in China and in Korea, in India, doing these kinds of things, and you’re right. I mean, as a Western parent, it is really surprising. When you talk to the parents and you ask them what they went through, you really start to understand that this is their decision, and I have great sympathy for the parents who do this, as well as the kids. The kids are really confused, of course, because they’re just children. Rosin: Right. It’s so interesting to hear you talk about this, because I know that you exist in the tradition of social-realist novels of the 19th century, and there is an element of maybe social justice in that? Lee: Sure, sure. We’re from Queens! Rosin: We’re from Queens. We care about all the—we care about the underdogs. And I was wondering, is this like Upton Sinclair social justice? Like, I’m trying to expose the sort of crushing capitalist pressures that produce something like Ginny ? But that’s not really your tone, even though that’s, you know, a mode that you exist in. Your tone is a little more anthropologist. Lee: Yeah. I think you’re so smart to pick up on that, because there’s a part of me that wants to be the muckraker. But people don’t wanna read it. Rosin: Interesting. Lee: Yeah. Nobody wants that. Nobody wants the sermon. You know what people want? They want entertainment. And through entertainment and through drama, people will start to think, Oh, I really feel bad for this kid, Ginny. She’s 9 years old. She’s being parachuted . And all of a sudden, you become Ginny, ’cause that’s what fiction does. ’Cause you identify with somebody in the scene. You’re like, Well, how would that feel to be Ginny? And I’m actually saying, I want you to think about Ginny, but I also want you to think about the guardian. Asian parenting often becomes pathologized. It’s decontextualized. All we can see is the outcome, or we can see the data around it, but we don’t see the human interest. And as a matter of fact, if you were in the same situation, you might actually make the same decision. Rosin: What drew you to this subject after Pachinko ? Why education? Why did that become the thing that you thought was important to explore? Lee: So I’m gonna write this thing called Diaspora Quartet . All the books are not related in characters or plot, but they’re related by this idea of diaspora because I think diaspora is now the modern person’s permanent condition. Rosin: Interesting. What do you mean? Everybody? Lee: Everybody. Not just Koreans, everybody. So for example, environmental diaspora, right? So you don’t have any water in your city, in your town, and you have to move. You don’t have any more jobs in your town, so you have to move. If you wanna go get an education or you have to cross a border. And I’m saying that we are being scattered by modern society, so we have to study the subject. Like, I think we’ve gotta take it really seriously. So my entire novelistic work before I quit is going to be diaspora. The people that I look at are Koreans. That’s my lane. It’s a lane I really wanna be in. And after my first two books, I asked myself, What is the value that Koreans care about more than any other thing? Because, and I took it really based upon all my interviews. I’ve had thousands of interviews, and in every single one of them, they talk about education with this kind of controversial kind of take. They all care about the subject, but they have such different opinions on it that it always kinda took my breath away, because it was so not American. And that’s all I can say. It’s like, it was so unfamiliar to me, at the same time so familiar, because I heard it over and over again. Rosin: And how—what is it? How would you summarize it? Lee: That they care about it more than religion. They care more about it than money. They care more about it than status. Rosin: Like, it’s almost a faith. Lee: Yes. Yes. Rosin: Like, they believe it is a token to success, almost in a pachinko way of, like, If you get this token, everything will work out . Lee: Everything will work out, and also, it means so much to another person—like, if we learn, Oh, Hanna went to this school . I’m talking middle school. I’m not even talking about college here. Like, you went to this middle school. It means that you were in certain neighborhoods, and you’re, let’s say, the top student, ’cause they have that. They will remember the top student of a middle school. And consequently, that means something to your classmates who went to middle school with you. And I think the average American person would say, “That is insane.” ( Laughs .) Rosin: Right. Right. We don’t think of it as a belief in that way. Like, an absolute belief. Lee: Yeah. You know? So, I mean, and it wasn’t all the Koreans, but I would find Koreans who would say these things, and I thought, Huh, that’s so interesting . So I thought, Okay, I’m gonna write this book about education, and I’m going to connect it with diaspora , because it made a lot of sense to me, because they would always say, “I wanna go here to learn English for my kid.” And they would accept all these arrangements, like the parachute kid. Like the wild-geese phenomenon, which is when the father stays home, earns all the money, and the mom and the kid live somewhere else, like Australia, like the Philippines, in order to learn English. And people don’t really know that there are Koreans everywhere— Rosin: Yeah. Lee: —especially where English is spoken. And you wouldn’t—and it’s not so obvious why they go. Rosin: Yeah. So you’re both examining this idea and a little bit pushing back against this idea. Lee: I wanna figure it out, and then I also wanna be fair to it, ’cause there’s two things. One is I don’t think in America we talk enough about education. We’re not helping children get the skills they need to take care of themselves. That is— Rosin: Like, we’re failing in education. Lee: We’re failing. Rosin: We don’t worship it enough, or we don’t believe in it enough. Lee: Like, if we have Koreans who are doing things at this sort of intense rate, we are doing that almost as a nation. We’re falling behind. Rosin: In a too lackadaisical way. In fact, I would say the mythology that’s taken hold at this moment in America is the opposite. You’re wasting your time . Like, what you really should be doing is leaving your education and going to be an entrepreneur or a tech entrepreneur. Like, it’s like you’re a chump if you stick to the rote path. Lee: Well, also this whole chump-ness, the chump population, the fact that we can even call people chumps is so anti-intellectual. Like, which intellectual person would just say, “Oh, you’re a chump for getting a Ph.D.”? That you would study eight years to get a doctorate. Right? ’Cause the tech bros would be like, “You’re clearly a ding-dong, because I quit college.” Not all the tech bros, obviously, but I think that kind of thinking is—in Korea, if you have a Ph.D., that’s considered very honorable. By most people. Not everybody, but by many. Rosin: I was thinking of a specific scene in the novel. It’s this community gathering at a Christian church, and one of the main characters, whose name is Lion, is giving this big speech to all of the parents. Lion runs this very successful Hagwon business that caters to Korean immigrants in Los Angeles. And in his speech, he’s telling the parents, Will you please worry less about your kids’ grades and less about where they’re going to college, and more about their mental health? He’s essentially pushing back against all this intensity. It’s an interesting scene for a lot of reasons: (1) It doesn’t really work. Like, it just makes him sort of more valuable and ups the parents’ panic. And (2) it’s interesting because, like, he’s running a hagwon, so I’m not really sure how to under—it’s almost like the leaders of the AI companies who are like, Please restrain us . Like, he’s in charge of it, you know? So I was curious to hear you talk about that scene. Lee: You know, I met all these hagwon teachers who had been doing it for a long time, and the ones who have been doing it for a long time, the ones who are really good, they’re almost like teenage whisperers, because these young kids, they don’t feel heard. Rosin: Yeah. Lee: They’re told a lot of things, but they’re not heard. So when you have this magical person who went to the famous school that your parents want you to go to, and they really listen to you, and they ask you questions like, So why do you wanna go to college? Maybe it’s not a good time . And the kid’s like, What do you mean? I have a choice? And they get really excited. And I think when you can have access to what the kids are really thinking, it’s a very privileged position. And then I think these teachers start to really identify with the young people more, and they’re trying to help them. Because what ends up happening is some of these kids do go to these schools, and then after the first year, they literally just crash. And they’re also exhausted, especially in America. Because when you have 14 AP classes, no one should be doing that. Rosin: Okay, that’s actually very helpful because the hagwon where a lot of the action takes place, the one run by Lion, is essentially—what it stands for is not a bucking of the system or a resistance. What it stands for is connection. Like, it’s a place where it’s an idealized form of tutoring and education, like, almost a connection between teacher and student. I have no idea if that exists or is common among hagwons, but that’s what novelistically it represents. Lee: I saw hagwon teachers. Overwhelmingly, they’re pretty decent people. But I have met hagwon teachers who do bad things, who cheat. Rosin: Who help the children cheat. Like they teach them bad values. Lee: Yeah, or they write the college essays. They just take the parents’ money, and they churn these things out, and they also—the worst thing I think they do by cheating is by telling the kids, “This is the way the world works. So you carry on, and you keep doing this.” Rosin: Right. So it makes them cynical. Lee: Oh, the young people right now are so cynical in a way that you and I are like innocent, so innocent at that age, because we did not know. I shouldn’t speak for you, Hanna, but most people that I knew at Bronx Science, we did not really understand a lot of things. Like, I didn’t know about legacies, for example. I didn’t know about having a famous parent. Like, I didn’t know about the sports track of how you get into school, especially at Bronx Science. There are so many things I didn’t know, and I think that when you figure out, actually, if there are 1,200 seats in a class for that college, really there are about 400 left for the general population. And of that, that needs to be divided among a global constituency. Rosin: Now that you do know all these things, you did go to elite colleges. Lee: I did. Yeah. Rosin: So when you look back, I mean, you went to some of the most prestigious universities, Yale and Georgetown. Did writing this book make you think differently about your experience in elite academia? Lee: Well, I think that when I went to these elite spaces, except for Bronx Science, where I really felt normal and happy—it’s New York, and it’s just other kids from the boroughs. And also, not that much was expected of me. Like, I didn’t have a lot of pressure at home to study and to become something. Rosin: Because your parents were not the so-called tiger parents. Lee: No. My mother’s very laissez-faire, ’cause she went to a very prestigious school in Korea, and she’s a music person, and her attitude is, “If you have the brains and you squander it, that’s on you.” Rosin: That’s nice. There’s freedom in that. Lee: There’s a lot of freedom in it, and there’s three of us. So her attitude is, well, you know, again, I was considered sort of the slower of the pack. Rosin: Yeah. Lee: So then I really, I just, I was left to sort of read the free books and eventually find my way. And I think when I went to college, I met all these kids who were so polished and sophisticated and suave, and they were so well traveled. They just knew things that I just didn’t know, and I remember feeling like, Oh, I don’t know that. I really don’t know that, and I’ve never been there, and I don’t know how to pronounce that . Like, there were so many things I had read but I didn’t know how to say. [ Break ] Rosin: The novel is bookended by two financial catastrophes: the 1997 IMF crisis in South Korea and the 2008 subprime-mortgage crisis in the U.S. Why was it important for you to set it in this time period? What kind of pressure, extra pressure does that create? Lee: Well, I wanna talk about now. I mean, I write social novels, and I think one of the things that we don’t wanna do is: We don’t wanna recognize the villains in our lives, because they’re not legible to us. Like, a financial crisis—we don’t understand how much damage it does to all of us all the time, because we don’t wanna understand the subjects. Rosin: I see. So it’s easy to understand, like, a bad parent who ships—that’s very concrete. Lee: Yes, yes. Rosin: Yes, I see. Lee: Yeah. A bad parent, a war. Rosin: Yes. Lee: The other country. Rosin: Yeah. Lee: Right? A religious group that you don’t like. That’s very easy to say, Oh, it’s them. It’s not me . A financial crisis? We all actually participate in it. And we don’t wanna be responsible for learning about it. And, again, that’s education. I actually think that if we had personal-finance classes, it would make a humongous difference in the way America runs. Rosin: Just as in Pachinko , because of this financial crisis and other reasons, there are wild swings to family fortunes. What is interesting to you about putting your characters through that kind of suffering? What is important to learn about a family, or is that a way of testing people or evoking certain things? Lee: Well, it’s actually what happens to all of us. Somebody loses a job. When one parent loses a job or is, as we say, reduced , you wake up, you open your computer, and you get an email saying, Your division is gone . That’s America now. Rosin: Yeah. Lee: How does that affect your family? Especially if the parent is, let’s say, 47 or 52. It’s really difficult to start again— Rosin: Yeah. Lee: —at this age. And I wanted to show that happening to my characters because that’s what’s happening to us now. Rosin: Now, if that situation happens, there are a lot of directions: The family could break apart. People could get angry, violent. The family you feature, what’s remarkable about them is they almost immediately choose to sacrifice for each other. The father goes from corporate world to working in a fish-fry restaurant. The daughter, who’s really, really smart, decides, Oh, I’m gonna work and put my brothers through school . So it’s a lot of sacrifice. What’s interesting to you about sacrifice? Lee: Well, when I interviewed all these different families around the world about their education, especially the ones that lost everything in the IMF crisis, the ones who actually succeeded, the only survival strategy that worked was sacrifice and sequencing. Rosin: What do you mean? Is it sacrifice within the family context? Lee: Yeah. Somebody had to give. Not everybody’s gonna get what they want. Rosin: Uh-huh. Lee: And it may seem pretty logical and obvious, but if everybody tries to get what they want, then the entire unit breaks apart. Rosin: Yeah. I was wondering if you were working through the Korean concept or even a Christian concept of sacrifice. Lee: You know, it’s actually, I think there are religious aspects of it that I think are valuable, and it’s shared cross-culturally by families who have faith in a religion, but also it was just the only thing that’s gonna work, because there’s limited resources and limited time. So even if, take religion away, I think even economists would understand that sequencing is sometimes the only choice. Like, if you only have $100, and $40 is all you could spend for education, and you have, let’s say, three kids, you can’t do it for all the kids. Rosin: It’s funny, when you talk about some of these things or these decisions, you talk about the analytical part of them and less about the sort of spiritual, philosophical part of it. Like, in the book, the way sacrifice happens—I mean, there’s a lot of morality. Would you agree with that, that there is— Lee: I’m definitely a moral writer. Rosin: Yeah. Lee: I’m definitely a moral novelist. I mean, in the same way all the writers that I love are moral novelists. Actually, you know why? Because, actually, I think most people are desperate for morality. ( Laughs .) Rosin: And what do you mean by “morality”? ’Cause there’s one surface-level reading, which is that in this novel, family is really important and central, holds people together, and people really sacrifice for their families. And the one person who does things which are very patently, say, un-Christian—lie, steal, seduce married men—really gets her comeuppance. So that’s almost a traditional kind of morality. But maybe that’s not what you mean by morality. Lee: No. That’s actually just law. I mean, I was a former lawyer. Rosin: ( Laughs .) Yeah. Lee: So I have seen people who behave this way get in trouble. I’ve talked to a lot of white-collar-criminal lawyers. So it’s really interesting. So you can argue that in this current climate, that we should celebrate the antihero. We could, right? Rosin: And I would say a lot of Korean movies about inequality, at least the ones that are popular here, are very antihero, like Squid Game . I mean, they’re brutal and they don’t have any traditional morality. They definitely celebrate the antihero. Lee: Right. But so I know the director and the writer of that show, for example, and when we talk about politics, he’s a very moral person. Rosin: Interesting. Lee: I mean, the reason why you show that in a satirical way is because you’re so outraged by the inequality. I think Koreans are really outraged by unfairness. Like, if you wanna have a scandal in Korea as a politician, your kid cheats on something and you let it go, that actually becomes a national scandal. If your wife accepts a handbag and she shouldn’t have, that’s corruption. Rosin: That’s interesting, ’cause right now there’s sort of beginning to be a call for Democrats not to just talk about affordability, but to talk about how unfair things are. You know, to sort of add a kind of element of injustice and morality to what’s happening, which we see in data centers. It hasn’t quite percolated into the political language quite yet, but it’s there. When you said people are desperate for morality, what is in your head? What are you thinking about? Lee: Well, when I take the temperature of America right now with the people that I meet, people are really upset about the fact that we’re all so cynical, including children. Nobody believes in anything. And we think that terrible things are happening, and nobody’s being held accountable. Yet regular middle-class people still have to pay their bills, and we can’t ask questions why. Gas prices are going up. Egg prices are going up. The rent’s going up. There’s no house to buy. The interest rates are going up. So this affordability crisis is a lot about, Hey, this is not fair , because some people who have assets are doing great, ’cause the stock market, despite all these things, is artificially inflated, and it’s doing great. But if you’re the chump who doesn’t have assets, you’re really upset. Again, fairness. Rosin: Yeah. Lee: You know, I think most people really see themselves as decent. That’s the other thing. ’Cause I’ve interviewed a lot of people who do some crazy bad things, illegal things. And they always have a reason why. And they’ll say things like, I did it for my family. I did it for my mother . I did it for X, Y, Z . And you’re kind of going like, But it’s illegal . But they have a reason. And so when I listen to them, I go, Okay, well, most people really believe that they’re pretty decent . And then I meet people who are really trying to do the right thing with almost nothing. That always stuns me. Rosin: Yeah. So you’ve talked a little bit about the quartet here. The fourth book is gonna be called the Marshall Plan . It’s always terrible to ask someone: How’s it going? ( Laughs .) Lee: ( Laughs .) Rosin: I’m not even gonna ask. Lee: I started. Rosin: Oh, you did? Congratulations. Lee: Thank you. Rosin: Can you just talk a little bit about what you’re exploring in the Marshall Plan ? Lee: So I think that the Marshall Plan is probably the smartest, most moral thing America did. Rosin: Let’s just say what it is. Lee: Sure. Rosin: It’s the 1948 U.S. initiative to help with economic recovery in Europe after World War II. How’s that as a summary? Lee: Very, very. That’s— Rosin: Thank you. Lee: A+. Rosin: Okay. Lee: And the reason why that’s quite astonishing is because we could have taken the tack, Germany, you did something beyond evil. You should be punished. You should just suffer , right? But I think that people were aware that that suffering during World War I and the economic terms, which caused inflation and which caused this demagogue to become powerful, and then he scapegoated a minority, maybe we don’t wanna do that again. And by rebuilding—and rebuilding by giving money to Europe—all of us benefited, America and Europe. So it’s this thing that I think we always turn to in saying, We could do that . Rosin: Yeah. Lee: Why don’t we do that again? Why do we always like hurting people? I’m writing something called, Marshall Plan , not the Marshall Plan. And it’s about this idea of remittances and reconstruction. So all these Koreans left Korea in the ’60s and ’70s, and they went to Germany to work as miners and nurses, about 20,000 of them. And they sent their deutsche marks back to South Korea to help rebuild the country. And then also, many Koreans went to Europe and became artists and learned more about the arts in Europe: singers, violinists, filmmakers, photographers. And then also, many women married GIs and went to America, and they sent money back to South Korea. I’m interested in this idea of remittances. Rosin: I’m seeing—as you’re talking, I think I’m getting a better sense because it’s not a quartet in that we’re following the same characters over time, but you are thinking very hard about the world as it is, kind of different ways that it could be. Lee: Yes. Rosin: And morality in a sort of complex way, because it’s a morality that is constrained and exists in a very realistic world. Like, a world in which no one’s really dealt a fair hand, in which bad things happen, and particularly to people who don’t have that much power. Lee: Yeah. Rosin: You know? Lee: No, you’re getting it. You’re really getting it. And it’s so important to me, because I’m not that interested in pointing out problems. I’m trying to figure out what works, and what has worked for people who have very little. Because all I hear all the time is that the world is burning down. And I’m thinking, like, This is not what we tell college students or teenagers. It’s not something that we tell middle-aged people . ( Laughs .) Rosin: You mean because it’s not inspiring? Lee: Because (1) it’s also not true. It’s not true. If you look at the history of the world, things are horrible now, but they’re also—it was horrible then. And in some ways, significantly more horrible then. For women, right? All the illnesses that we’ve cured since then. And I keep thinking, Well, how did all of our ancestors deal with these horrific problems of just foolishness and hatred? All of it . And we need to figure something out, and we need to remember, because I know that this, like, perpetual state of fear and anxiety is not something that we can—like, we can’t do this. We have to have another story. [ Music ] Rosin: This is so good because I think a lot of people in this moment in American history take the path of avoidance or distraction. And you are essentially writing or speaking an intellectual’s guide to a happy life. Like, a high-information guide to a happy life. So I appreciate it. Well, Min, thank you so much for joining me. And congratulations. Lee: Well, Hanna, now that I know that we’re twins. ( Laughs .) Rosin: Yeah. I know, I kinda wish I’d gone to Bronx Science, you know? [ Music ] Rosin: This episode of Radio Atlantic was produced by Rosie Hughes and Jinae West. It was edited by Kevin Townsend. Yvonne Kim fact-checked. Rob Smierciak engineered and provided original music. We also had music from Breakmaster Cylinder. Claudine Ebeid is the executive producer of Atlantic audio, and Andrea Valdez is our managing editor. Listeners, if you enjoy the show, you can support our work and the work of all Atlantic journalists when you subscribe to The Atlantic at TheAtlantic.com/Listener . I’m Hanna Rosin. Thank you for listening.

items.title: US: Nebraskans Losing Coverage as Medicaid Changes
items.description: Nebraska’s efforts to implement new, federally mandated work requirements for Medicaid underscore fears that millions of people will experience avoidable barriers to healthcare coverage.Federal authorities could have chosen to blunt the impact of the federal legislation’s Medicaid cuts. Instead, they added even more convoluted requirements that will deprive people of health care they are entitled to.Nebraska is the canary in the coal mine for issues that most states will face when they begin implementing these work requirements. As they do, they should make sure red tape doesn’t strip people of health care. (Washington, DC) – Nebraska’s efforts to implement new, federally mandated work requirements for Medicaid underscore fears that millions of people will experience avoidable barriers to healthcare coverage, Human Rights Watch, Oxfam America, and Nebraska Appleseed said today. On May 1, 2026, Nebraska became the first state to implement work requirements for Medicaid, the public health insurance program for people with low- or no-income, as part of public spending cuts mandated by the Trump administration’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA), which also extended and deepened tax cuts that overwhelmingly benefit high-income households and corporations. These new rules will require most adults without dependents to document at least 80 hours per month of work, education, or other approved activities to maintain Medicaid coverage. States must implement the requirements by January 1, 2027, though they may do so sooner, as Nebraska has. “Nebraska is the canary in the coal mine for issues that most states will face when they begin implementing these work requirements,” said Matt McConnell, US researcher on economic, social, and cultural rights at Human Rights Watch. “As they do, they should make sure red tape doesn’t strip people of health care.” Human Rights Watch and Oxfam America in August and September interviewed a dozen Nebraskans with personal or professional experience with Medicaid and a public employee involved in the process. People interviewed said that the state’s rollout of new work requirements increased administrative burdens and risked disruptions in access to health care following the rushed implementation of these federal requirements. Data suggests that large numbers of people are already losing coverage in Nebraska because of the work requirements. Eli McCreary, age 64 at the time, said he lost his Medicaid coverage while undergoing treatment for kidney cancer and multiple chronic health conditions. He said a representative of the health plan that managed his Medicaid coverage informed him he lost access because he was not working, even though he is unable to work due to his condition. “If I could work, I would work,” he said. “But I can’t…. I can’t walk around. I mean, I can’t breathe. I can’t walk very far.” The sudden lapse in coverage disrupted his planned care. “I was supposed to go see the cancer specialist here…. And that date was canceled, so I couldn’t. I had to wait until I got insurance again to even come back out here.... Everything was delayed.” A Medicaid eligibility worker from the Nebraska Department of Health and Human Services said that poor training, vague and inconsistent guidance, and technical issues, including unprepared software systems, had caused stress and uncertainty for applicants and for state employees. “We just sometimes don’t know what we’re doing,” the worker said, describing the rollout as rushed and confusing. “I wish the people who make policies knew what they were doing.” The OBBBA, which became law in July 2025, imposed new eligibility criteria on the nearly 20 million adults without dependents in the 40 states and the District of Columbia who rely on expanded Medicaid coverage under the Affordable Care Act. Nebraska expanded coverage through a ballot initiative in 2018. Adults in this expansion population will be required to prove that they either satisfy these new work requirements or qualify for a statutory exemption, including for caregivers of young children, pregnant people, certain people with disabilities, and those deemed medically frail. States may also choose to offer short-term hardship exceptions for certain individuals, such as those in counties with a federally declared emergency or disaster. The Urban Institute estimated that between 3 and 7 million people in the United States could lose Medicaid coverage by 2028 because of these new requirements. The Congressional Budget Office, a nonpartisan government research agency, estimated that work requirements would increase the number of uninsured people in the United States by 4.8 million by 2034. Nebraska Appleseed, a Lincoln-based nonprofit advocacy organization, has repeatedly requested data from the state regarding its implementation of these requirements. On September 29, 2026, Nebraska publicly released initial figures showing that over 1,000 people lost or were denied Medicaid coverage under the new requirements between May and August of this year. The number of people affected is likely to grow significantly over the coming months as state officials review enrollees’ eligibility on a rolling basis. “Getting data from the state about how many people are losing coverage and why shouldn’t be like pulling teeth,” said Sarah Maresh, healthcare access program director at Nebraska Appleseed. “Nebraskans deserve access to this information. You can’t fix problems you refuse to measure.” In May, Human Rights Watch and Oxfam America warned that millions of people were at risk of losing coverage due to the work requirements. In a joint letter to the US Department of Health and Human Services and the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS), the organizations urged federal authorities to issue guidance for states that would help prevent these new federal requirements from causing harmful and unnecessary Medicaid denials and terminations. But CMS issued binding guidance on June 1 that will require burdensome case-by-case assessments. “Federal authorities could have chosen to blunt the impact of the OBBBA’s inequality-fueling Medicaid cuts,” said Jackson Gandour, senior economic justice policy adviser at Oxfam America. “Instead, they added even more convoluted requirements that will deprive people of the health care they are entitled to.” Under international human rights law, everyone has the right to the highest attainable standard of physical and mental health. Medicaid eligibility requirements already exclude people who earn too much to meet extremely low-income eligibility limits but not enough to afford private health insurance. Complex work reporting requirements may exclude millions more, undermining their rights to health, social security, and an adequate standard of living. Because the rules largely affect people with low incomes, these losses may also deepen inequality, the organizations said. Officials in Nebraska and other states preparing to implement the work requirement provisions should identify ways to reduce administrative burdens and simplify eligibility assessments. Officials should also take steps to strengthen existing exemptions; improve communication about, and understanding of, who is subject to work requirements and who is exempt; and enhance transparency by regularly publishing data on application denials, coverage terminations, appeals, reinstatements, and the reasons underlying these decisions. “Work requirements are a solution in search of a problem,” McConnell said. “The truth is that they make life harder for people who are already working or can’t work.” Widespread Confusion; Risk of Disrupted Care People currently on Medicaid expressed confusion about whether work requirements or relevant exemptions applied to them, and what steps they needed to take to maintain coverage. “I got a letter early in January stating that the work requirements were coming, and then basically, that’s it,” said Schmeeka Simpson, a 44-year-old community organizer in Omaha and mother of three. She said she received a letter informing her that she was approved for Medicaid in August, but with no explanation for how Nebraska determined she complied with the work requirements. “I’m like ‘great, that’s wonderful,’ but I don't know how they came to those conclusions.” Due to the lack of clarity, Simpson said, it is difficult to know how to maintain Medicaid eligibility. “Who, what, when, where, why, and how hasn’t been answered…. These are life and death situations for people. This is not just politics.” Melissa Craig, a single mother in Omaha who relies on Medicaid, said she only learned that she qualified for an exemption to work requirements shortly before they went into effect: “It is very stressful for me on a day-to-day basis about what my future and my son’s future looks like. Staying on top of it is a full-time job.” Megan Word, government relations director covering Nebraska and Kansas for American Cancer Society Cancer Action Network (ACS CAN), said “The workers can’t even quickly identify whether somebody is on the expansion population or not.” She said even Medicaid eligibility workers may be unaware of whether someone will be subject to work requirements. “The biggest concern is the administrative burden that is going to be placed on ... the patient,” said Amy Behnke, who leads the Health Center Association of Nebraska, which represents the seven healthcare providers operating federally qualified health centers in Nebraska. She said: “Prior to Medicaid expansion, our health centers had a 50 percent uninsured rate, and now we’re down to about a third. So, expansion has been incredibly significant to our health centers and to their patients … [But] often what we see with patients is that … they’re working sometimes multiple jobs, they’re taking care of their families, they’re figuring out how to put food on their table. And so, any time you ask somebody to take one more step when it comes to verifying their health insurance, the higher the likelihood is that something is going to fall through the cracks.” She described a recent case at one of the centers she represents. A pregnant woman arrived for a prenatal appointment and learned she no longer had Medicaid coverage, despite being exempt from work requirements. Eventually staff determined that state officials had overlooked a box indicating she was pregnant and the woman was able to regain Medicaid coverage, but it took multiple calls and she had to reschedule appointments. “This never should have been an issue,” Behnke said. Confusion surrounding work requirements may also discourage otherwise eligible people from applying for Medicaid coverage. “I had three different patients outright tell me, ‘What’s the point of enrolling? I’m not employed,’” said a licensed social worker based in Omaha who like some others spoke on condition of anonymity. She stressed that working with a social worker was essential to getting these people to apply. “It really, in our experience, becomes a game of how connected you are to a caseworker who can write these accommodations or write these letters and verify your status. And it really just becomes, just kind of a dice roll of privilege, unfortunately.” This confusion may already be causing disruptions in care. McCreary, the Omaha man who lost coverage while undergoing cancer treatment, learned that he had lost Medicaid coverage from his healthcare providers. “Unless you’re going to self-pay, we can’t take you, because your insurance canceled out,” he said, describing his conversation with hospital staff. “I had to cancel all of my appointments.” He said that when he contacted the managed care organization that administered his Medicaid coverage, he was informed that he had lost coverage because he was not working. “They said, you’re not working. I can’t really do anything for you.” Administrative Capacity and Perverse Incentives Implementing these work requirements involves creating new administrative processes within state agencies overseeing Medicaid, as well as training for the public employees who administer them, the organizations said. The federal law also requires all states, starting in January 2027, to increase the frequency of eligibility redeterminations from once per year, as required by the federal Affordable Care Act, to every six months. While this will effectively double the number of eligibility determinations the department must process each year, staffing is not keeping up with the increased workload. In the December 2025 news conference to announce that Nebraska would be the first state to implement work requirements under the OBBBA, Governor Jim Pillen said that no extra staff would be hired to help track work requirements. In July, Nebraska instituted a hiring freeze for state agencies including the health department citing a state budget shortfall that has been worsened by a 2023 law that nearly halved Nebraska’s tax rate for the highest earners. One Medicaid eligibility worker said that capacity issues, along with internal bureaucratic incentives, exacerbate the risk that eligible people will be denied coverage. They said chronic understaffing and pressure to clear cases is compounded by confusion and a lack of adequate training around the eligibility changes: “We just sometimes don’t know what we are doing … and then you have [Medicaid applicants] coming in, understandably they’re upset.” They said staff had recently been required to revisit some cases because supervisors had relayed incorrect information. “The supervisors were told something wrong and told us something wrong and now we’re having to go back and fix all these cases.” The worker said they face pressure to increase the number of cases closed. “You have to get your numbers up,” the worker said, relaying the message they and other staff regularly get from managers. “That’s really messed up because denials are the easiest.” This prioritizes speed over accuracy, the worker said, incentivizing staff to rapidly deny applications if there is any cause and disincentivizing staff from spending the time necessary to correct apparent errors, omissions, or inquiring more about potential pathways to coverage through existing exemptions. “All of that work that you do to try to verify, it doesn’t count. So, it looks like you did nothing,” the worker said. “All I think about is numbers and getting it done. I get so anxious and nervous.” Rushed and Unclear Implementation In Nebraska’s rush to be the first state to implement the work requirements, it developed eligibility criteria before official federal guidance was issued. The result has been a mismatch between the state and federal eligibility rules. “Nebraska went live with their work requirement implementation on May 1 and the Feds published their [mandatory guidance] on June 1,” said Megan Word of the ACS CAN. “[Nebraska] did not pause. They did not say, ‘Wait a minute … we need to review the differences,’ because there were many.” She said before the federal government issued mandatory guidance in June, through the Interim Final Rule, Nebraska had created a list of medical codes for diagnoses that might automatically satisfy the “medically frail” exemption to work requirements written into the OBBBA. “If you can find one of those medical conditions on the list, then theoretically, you should be eligible for an exemption,” Word said. However, this was inconsistent with the federal rule. Under that rule, a diagnosis such as cancer does not automatically establish an exemption, leaving many people who are unable to work because of their health unsure of whether they remain eligible for Medicaid. Instead, the federal rule defines “medically frail” as a “physical, mental, or other behavioral health condition [that] significantly impairs the individual’s ability to comply” with work requirements. “The Interim Final Rule makes it harder for patients to obtain this exemption,” Word said, because it puts the burden of proving one’s inability to work on enrollees, while also requiring a case-by-case review from implementing agencies. “That will involve some sort of independent verification, a process that no one really understands at this point.” For the time being, Nebraska is allowing people to submit a declaration—“self-attest”—that they are “medically frail” without having to provide additional supporting documentation. Human Rights Watch and Oxfam America recommended that federal authorities should help enable self-attestation in its May letter. Although the rules published in June allowed states to accept self-attestation for an exemption from work requirements, it only allows states to do so until January 2028, after which states will only be allowed to accept self-attestation when documentation is not “reasonably available.” In practice, both a lack of awareness regarding the availability of these exemptions and a broad misunderstanding about who may be eligible for them undermines the temporary availability of self-attestation, the groups found. People who may be unable to work because of their health must also juggle bureaucratic hurdles to prove their eligibility, frequently while undergoing sometimes intensive medical treatment. According to KFF, a nonpartisan health policy research organization, more than 6 out of every 10 people under age 65 on Medicaid are already working full or part time. About 3 out of 10 are not working because of caregiving responsibilities, disability, or illness, or because they are attending school. Fewer than 1 in 10 are unemployed for another reason, including retirement or the inability to find work. “Why are you putting in work requirements when the majority of people who rely on Medicaid are already working anyway?” Word said. Lessons from Georgia Human Rights Watch and Oxfam America’s joint research in the state of Georgia—which in 2023 expanded Medicaid coverage to adults without dependents but conditioned eligibility on meeting work requirements similar to those in OBBBA—indicate that work requirements compound existing barriers to accessing health care. According to data provided by the state to the Georgia Budget & Policy Institute, a nonprofit advocacy organization, over 100,000 people are estimated to be eligible for Georgia’s Medicaid expansion, but as of August 2026, only 20,321 were enrolled. According to the latest data published by the state of Georgia, about half of the 17,638 denials for their Medicaid expansion program between October 2024 and September 2025 were due to a failure to either meet or verify compliance with work requirements. Lack of Transparency Because Nebraska has been slow to release data on the impact of work requirements on Medicaid enrollment, advocates have struggled to assess the impacts of these policies. “We’re flying blind,” Behnke said. Without detailed data, health centers cannot identify where patients are losing coverage or adjust outreach strategies effectively. OBBBA’s Disproportionate Impact on Low-Income Households The addition of work requirements to Medicaid was among a series of provisions in OBBBA that reduced federal spending on public services and programs, including through restrictive eligibility and reporting requirements. These reductions were designed in part to offset tax cuts that disproportionately benefit high-income households and corporations. The nonpartisan Congressional Joint Committee on Taxation found that the top 0.1 percent of earners will receive an average tax cut of $311,000 in 2027 because of the OBBBA, while taxes will increase for the lowest-income households. The Congressional Budget Office found that the OBBBA’s Medicaid work requirements will reduce federal spending by $326 billion over the next decade. Meanwhile, the total cost of the OBBBA’s tax breaks for corporations and the wealthiest 1 percent of households is estimated at around $2 trillion.

Nuit de la RPP : Des milliers de Burkinabè réunis pour célébrer la Révolution
items.description: À l'occasion de la Nuit de la Révolution progressiste populaire (RPP), marquant l'an 4 de l'arrivée au pouvoir du capitaine Ibrahim Traoré, le Premier ministre Rimtalba Jean Emmanuel Ouédraogo s'est adressé aux Burkinabè d'ici et d'ailleurs, ce mercredi 30 septembre 2026, à la Place de la Révolution à Ouagadougou. Des milliers de citoyens, venus des différentes régions du pays, ont pris part à cette mobilisation placée sous le signe de l'engagement patriotique et de la poursuite de la lutte contre le terrorisme. La Place de la Révolution a connu une forte affluence dans la nuit du mercredi 30 septembre 2026. Filles et fils du Burkina Faso, militants et sympathisants panafricanistes se sont mobilisés pour commémorer les quatre années écoulées de leadership du Capitaine Ibrahim Traoré à la tête du pays des Hommes intègres. Prenant la parole à cette occasion, le Premier ministre, Rimtalba Jean Emmanuel Ouédraogo, a salué une « mobilisation exceptionnelle » des Burkinabè. « C'est une mobilisation exceptionnelle des filles et fils dans toutes les régions du Burkina Faso. C'est une mobilisation des panafricanistes convaincus », a-t-il déclaré. Rimtalba Jean Emmanuel Ouédraogo, Premier ministre, Chef du gouvernement « Quatre ans après, le Burkina Faso n'est plus le même » Pour le chef du gouvernement, les quatre dernières années doivent être appréciées à l'aune des faits et des changements intervenus dans le pays. « Quatre ans après, les faits de l'histoire nous donnent raison. Quatre ans après, le Burkina Faso n'est plus le même. Quatre ans après, le Burkina Faso respire. Quatre ans après, le Burkina Faso espère et est convaincu que les jours du terrorisme sont comptés », a affirmé Rimtalba Jean Emmanuel Ouédraogo. Le Premier ministre a également appelé les Burkinabè à apprécier la situation nationale à partir des réalités vécues plutôt qu'à travers les seuls discours. La soirée à connu la présence d'éminentes personnalités « Quatre ans après, nous ne demandons à qui que ce soit de croire au discours ou à un serment. Nous demandons seulement de regarder les faits », a-t-il insisté. Hommage aux héros et appel à poursuivre la lutte Cette Nuit de la Révolution a également été présentée comme un moment de recueillement et de mobilisation. « Cette nuit de la RPP est une halte pour rendre hommage à nos héros et pour faire le plein d'énergie, car la lutte continue », a indiqué le Premier ministre. Selon lui, les défis restent nombreux et la vigilance demeure nécessaire. Il a notamment déclaré que « l'impérialiste ne baisse pas les bras », tout en affirmant que celui-ci « connaîtra toujours l'échec ici, sur la terre libre de nos ancêtres, le Burkina Faso ». Hommage a été rendu aux FDS et VDP Dans son intervention, Rimtalba Jean Emmanuel Ouédraogo a également insisté sur la détermination des autorités et de ceux qui adhèrent à leur démarche. « Nous avançons convaincus et nous allons avancer avec les convaincus. Quand quelqu'un fait semblant de dormir, il n'y a aucune chance de le réveiller », a-t-il lancé. Le chef du gouvernement a enfin appelé à la vigilance face aux menaces qui, selon lui, continuent de peser sur le pays. « Nos ennemis sont connus, ce sont les impérialistes assoiffés de nos ressources. Il faut être vigilant pour ne jamais être surpris », a déclaré le Premier ministre. La Nuit de la Révolution s'est ainsi inscrite dans un contexte de commémoration, d'hommage aux combattants tombés et de mobilisation autour des enjeux sécuritaires et de souveraineté nationale. La soirée a été marquée par de nombreuses prestations d'artiste du Burkina Faso et de la sous région. Jean-François SOMÉ Sakinatou ZOUNDI Minute.bf

items.title: Souveraineté cacaoyère: la meilleure thèse de Dschang valide le modèle agroforestier du Cameroun
items.description: © DR Comment produire plus de cacao sans raser la forêt ? La meilleure thèse de Doctorat 2025-2026 de la Dschang School of Agricultural and Environmental Sciences répond avec des chiffres. Soutenue le 28 février 2026 par le Dr Romuald Duplex Djeuni, elle démontre que les systèmes agroforestiers du Moungo sont des modèles durables qui peuvent concilier souveraineté agricole et exigences du marché mondial. C'est l'équation politique de la décennie pour le Cameroun, deuxième producteur africain de cacao. Comment préserver la rente de cette matière première stratégique face à la nouvelle réglementation européenne sur la déforestation importée qui menace nos exportations ? La réponse vient des laboratoires de l'Université de Dschang. La thèse du Dr Romuald Duplex Djeuni, intitulée « Analyse du fonctionnement et de la dynamique des services écosystémiques des systèmes agroforestiers à base de cacaoyers dans le département du Moungo », a été sacrée meilleure thèse 2025-2026 de l'École doctorale. Les travaux, co-dirigés par les Pr Lucie Félicité Temgoua et Marie Caroline Momo Solefack et soutenus devant le Pr Christopher Tankou, relèvent de la gestion intégrée des ressources forestières. Pendant 18 mois, de juin 2022 à novembre 2023, le chercheur a sillonné Loum, Njombé-Penja et Mbanga, interrogé 118 producteurs et inventorié les parcelles. Le verdict est politique : nos cacaoyères traditionnelles sont déjà vertueuses. Les résultats plaident pour l'agroforesterie comme modèle souverain. Les parcelles abritent 52 espèces d'arbres issues de 27 familles, dont quatre vulnérables sur la liste rouge de l'UICN comme le Garcinia kola. Avec 109 arbres associés par hectare, bien au-delà des 42 à 60 recommandés en Afrique centrale, elles présentent un « potentiel élevé de conservation de la biodiversité ». Mieux, elles sont rentables écologiquement et économiquement. Elles stockent 91,39 tonnes de carbone par hectare, valorisées à 1 797 876 FCFA l'hectare, et assurent sept usages aux familles paysannes. Le rendement atteint 715,20 kg par hectare. L'étude nuance toutefois : au-delà d'un seuil, la densité d'arbres associés fait baisser le nombre de cabosses par cacaoyer. D'où la recommandation centrale du Dr Djeuni, titulaire d'une Licence en Géographie (2017) et d'un Master en Agroforesterie (2019) à Dschang, et formé au CIRAD et CIFOR-ICRAF. Il conseille aux producteurs de réguler les densités et de créer les cacaoyères sur jachères plutôt qu'en forêt. À l'État et aux instituts de recherche, il demande de certifier ces pratiques durables pour assurer traçabilité et reproductibilité via des formations adaptées. Enfin, il invite l'Union européenne à reconnaître officiellement ces agroforêts comme conformes à sa norme « zéro déforestation ». Une thèse qui offre à l'État un argument scientifique massif pour défendre le cacao camerounais sur la scène internationale. Cet article Souveraineté cacaoyère: la meilleure thèse de Dschang valide le modèle agroforestier du Cameroun est apparu en premier sur Journalducameroun.com .

items.title: Los Reyes visitarán Ceuta y Melilla los días 13 y 14 de octubre
items.description: 13 y 14 de octubre. Esos serán los días en los que el rey Felipe VI y Letizia Ortiz visiten Ceuta y Melilla, según han informado este jueves fuentes de la Casa del Rey y de La Moncloa. Viaje al que no les acompañará el presidente del Gobierno, Pedro Sánchez, según han adelantado desde el Ejecutivo a la agencia Efe y ha confirmado este periódico. Las fechas se habían convertido en el secreto de Estado mejor guardado de los últimos tiempos. Después de dos meses de elucubraciones, expectativas y rifirrafes entre el Gobierno de Ceuta, el Ejecutivo central y Zarzuela, el calendario queda por fin despejado, además, antes de que todos los mandatarios civiles y militares coincidan, con motivo de los fastos de la fiesta nacional, el próximo 12 de octubre. items.title: Aéroport d’Alger : il déclare 65.000 $, « oublie » 3.800 € et se fait prendre
items.description: Déclarer une somme en devises pour mieux en dissimuler une autre peut être un stratagème efficace pour tromper la vigilance des contrôles aux frontières. Mais ça ne marche pas à tous les coups. Un habitué des voyages vers l'Espagne a été arrêté à l'aéroport d’Alger en possession illégale d'une somme en euro, alors qu’il a déclaré aux douaniers une importante somme en dollars. L’affaire a été jugée devant le tribunal de Dar El Beida. Selon un compte-rendu de l’audience fait par Ennahar, le mis en cause voyage fréquemment vers l’Espagne où il acquiert des confiseries à revendre en Algérie. Lors de l’un de ses voyages, il a déclaré aux services des douanes la somme de 65 000 euros. Mais après une fouille, il s'est avéré qu'il tentait de faire passer plus que cette somme. Les agents ont trouvé sur lui 3800 euros qu’il n’a pas déclaré dont il n'a pas pu justifier la provenance. Dollars déclarés et euros dissimulés à l’aéroport d’Alger : l’accusé plaide l’oubli Selon la loi algérienne, les montants que peuvent transporter sans être déclarés aux douanes sont plafonnés à 1000 euros. Au-delà, il faut déclarer et présenter un justificatif bancaire. Présenté devant le tribunal de Dar El Beida, l’homme est poursuivi pour violation de la législation et de la réglementation relatives aux mouvements de capitaux de et vers l'étranger. Son procès a eu lieu mercredi 30 septembre. Devant les juges, l’accusé a plaidé l’ “ oubli ”. Selon lui, il a simplement oublié de déclarer la somme en euros qu'il transportait. Dans sa stratégie de défense, il a tenté de convaincre le tribunal de sa bonne foi en soulignant qu'il voyage fréquemment à l'étranger et qu' il n'a jamais été pris en train de tenter de faire sortir illégalement des devises. Dans son réquisitoire, le parquet a requis une année de prison ferme et 100 000 dinars d'amende. items.title: Sahara marocain : Mike Waltz met le polisario face à l'évidence, les bases d'une solution existent
items.description: À New York, l'ambassadeur américain auprès de l'ONU, Mike Waltz, a reçu des représentants du polisario et leur a rappelé que « les bases d'une solution » existent déjà. Cet entretien a lieu à l'approche de la nouvelle échéance du Conseil de sécurité, dans le prolongement de la résolution 2797, qui a hissé l'initiative marocaine d'autonomie sous souveraineté marocaine au cœur du processus politique. L'ambassadeur des États-Unis auprès des Nations unies, Mike Waltz, a rencontré ce mercredi à New York une délégation du polisario, dans le cadre des consultations diplomatiques qui se poursuivent autour du dossier du Sahara marocain. À l'issue de l'entretien, le responsable américain a publié une photographie de la rencontre sur son compte officiel de la plateforme X, accompagnée d'un message centré sur la situation des populations des camps de Tindouf et sur la nécessité d'avancer vers une issue politique. « Les réfugiés des camps de Tindouf attendent depuis 50 ans. Ils méritent de vraies options, pas une décennie de plus d'attente. Les bases d'une solution existent » , a écrit Mike Waltz. Par cette déclaration, l'ambassadeur américain auprès de l'ONU insiste sur la durée du conflit et sur la nécessité de sortir du statu quo. La formule renvoie au cadre politique défendu à l'échelle internationale pour parvenir à un règlement définitif, à savoir l'initiative marocaine d'autonomie sous souveraineté marocaine. Cette rencontre s'inscrit dans un contexte de poursuite des efforts diplomatiques autour du processus onusien. Elle précède de quelques semaines l'examen annuel du dossier par le Conseil de sécurité, qui doit se prononcer fin octobre sur le renouvellement du mandat de la Minurso. Le cadre fixé par le Conseil de sécurité L'évolution récente du processus est notamment marquée par l'adoption de la résolution 2797 le 31 octobre 2025, qui a consacré l'initiative marocaine d'autonomie comme base des discussions en vue d'une solution politique. Le texte appelle les parties à avancer vers un règlement réaliste, pragmatique et durable, dans le cadre du processus conduit sous l'égide des Nations unies. Washington, qui joue un rôle central dans les discussions du Conseil de sécurité sur ce dossier en tant que rédacteur principal des projets de résolution, continue pour sa part d'encourager les parties à reprendre le dialogue politique. Plusieurs tours de consultations ont déjà réuni les acteurs concernés par le processus, notamment le Maroc, le Front séparatiste, l'Algérie et la Mauritanie. Ces échanges visent à relancer une dynamique de négociation après plusieurs années sans avancées substantielles. La rencontre entre Mike Waltz et la délégation du polisario s'inscrit ainsi dans une phase diplomatique où les discussions portent sur les moyens de parvenir à une solution politique conforme aux paramètres définis par les Nations unies. The post Sahara marocain : Mike Waltz met le polisario face à l'évidence, les bases d'une solution existent appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: Cameroun : 41 000 actes de naissance pour les enfants réfugiés et hôtes vulnérables de l’Est, de l’Adamaoua et du Nord
items.description: © DR Face au déficit persistant d'enregistrement des naissances, les acteurs de l'état civil et leurs partenaires se mobilisent pour une opération d'envergure : établir 41 000 actes de naissance au profit des enfants réfugiés et hôtes vulnérables des régions de l'Est, de l'Adamaoua et du Nord. La concertation préparatoire s'est tenue à Bertoua le mercredi 30 septembre 2026. L'objectif de la rencontre est d’harmoniser les stratégies, clarifier les responsabilités et jeter les bases d'une intervention coordonnée. Dans le seul département du Lom-et-Djérem, les données présentées font état de 14 074 actes à établir dans les arrondissements de Garoua-Boulaï, Bétaré-Oya, Ngoura, Mandjou, Bertoua 1er et Bertoua 2e. Présidés par le préfet du Lom-et-Djérem, Simon Nkwenti Ndoh, les travaux ont réuni autorités administratives, services déconcentrés de l'État, le Haut-commissariat des Nations Unies pour les réfugiés (HCR), le Bureau national de l’état civil (Bunec) et autres structures de la chaîne de l'état civil. À travers la présentation du projet par le chef de sous-délégation par intérim du HCR, René Guy Dagbo, les participants ont été édifiés sur les objectifs, les mécanismes et les étapes de l'opération. L'enjeu est de faciliter l'accès à l'identité juridique et, par ricochet, à plusieurs droits fondamentaux. Les échanges ont aussi porté sur les procédures de déclaration tardive, les réquisitions et les jugements déclaratifs. Le BUNEC, représenté par son chef d'agence régionale, Étienne Christian Bindzi Bindzi, a apporté des éclaircissements sur les mécanismes d'enregistrement et les impératifs de fiabilité des données. Les participants ont relevé les risques liés aux doublons, aux variations d'informations déclarées par les parents ou encore à la succession de plusieurs campagnes. Autant de problématiques qui appellent une coordination rigoureuse. L'opération, annoncée pour démarrer le 10 octobre 2026, entre ainsi dans une phase préparatoire décisive. items.title: UAE says investigation launched into diverted flydubai flight
items.description: The United Arab Emirates’ chief prosecutor on Thursday ordered an investigation into the incident aboard flydubai flight FZ1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv, which made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia after a reported altercation in the cockpit. The state news agency WAM said the attorney general had ordered the probe, adding that “the investigation team has launched its work into the incident” that forced the plane to land in Saudi Arabia on Wednesday. The investigation will examine the circumstances and motives, including whether it was linked to any militant activity or involved prior planning or direction. UAE judicial authorities have jurisdiction over the incident because the aircraft is registered in the UAE and flies under its flag, the statement said, adding that UAE law applies to crimes committed on board “even if they occur outside the country’s territory”. Passengers described rushing the cockpit after the plane suddenly plummeted, losing around 17,000 feet of altitude in the span of a minute, according to the Flightradar24 website. Airline flydubai said all the passengers — of whom 166 out of 174 were Israeli, according to media reports — were safe, adding that the reasons for the altercation were unknown. Netanyahu praises Indian pilot Meanwhile, Israel has alleged that the co-pilot of the flight had tried to crash the aircraft but that the pilot and passengers intervened and averted the crash. Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu credited the wounded pilot — identified as Indian national Smit Machchhar — and passengers of the flight, with Israeli officials terming the incident “an attempted terrorist attack”. Netanyahu hailed Smit’s “extraordinary bravery”, saying he fought off his copilot, preventing a “catastrophic mid-air disaster”. “During the flight, as they approached the country, one of the pilots stabbed the other pilot, and apparently tried to crash the plane with everyone on board,” Netanyahu claimed in a separate video message. In a Fox News interview, he also claimed an Israeli passenger helped overpower the attacker, identifying him only as Yanik and describing him as a plumber. “An amazing act of heroism — of his, of the Indian pilot, of the people who helped them. They stopped a disaster that could have been global,” Netanyahu insisted. The Indian embassy said Machchhar was being treated at a hospital in Saudi Arabia, and India’s Prime Minister Narendra Modi described him as a “HERO” in a social media post on Thursday. “His valour helped save hundreds of lives,” Modi said. Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar said he had spoken with his UAE counterpart Abdullah bin Zayed Al Nahyan and agreed “to collaborate against extremist elements seeking to harm security and undermine stability”. US President Donald Trump, after discussing the incident with Netanyahu, said: “It seems as though the co-pilot was perhaps a terrorist or perhaps a whack-job.” Riyadh turned down Israeli requests to send planes for passengers Saudi Arabia turned down multiple requests by Israel to send its own planes to retrieve passengers from the diverted flydubai flight, a Saudi source with knowledge of the matter told AFP on Thursday. “They asked to send military warplanes. Two or three direct to Tabuk airport,” the source told AFP . “Turned down.” “Then asked to send [El Al] commercial one. Turned down as well.” The source also told AFP the message was communicated through the UAE and not directly with the Israelis. The Saudi source said the kingdom fulfilled its “international obligation” and assisted the passengers of the flight after they made the emergency landing, emphasising that the nationality of the travellers had no impact on their decision. “We were to act the same way, regardless of the nationalities of flydubai passengers,” the source added. In recent years, Saudi Arabia has resisted pressure to join the US-backed Abraham Accords and establish diplomatic ties with Israel. Riyadh has maintained that it will not normalise relations with Israel without a clear path to Palestinian statehood. But the kingdom has long been seen as the most consequential potential addition to the Abraham Accords, with negotiations advancing at various points before stalling. ’Out of control’ AFPTV images showed another flydubai plane carrying the passengers touching down at Tel Aviv airport, hours after their initial flight was diverted to Saudi Arabia’s Tabuk. Footage shared by Netanyahu’s office showed the premier meeting passengers after their arrival in Tel Aviv and embracing a man in a bloodied shirt. Passenger Miryam Shira Ohayon described the plane as being “pretty much out of control” as the incident unfolded over Jordan. “The co-pilot tried to murder the pilot and basically carry out a suicide attack on the plane,” she told reporters by speakerphone held up by her mother at Ben Gurion Airport. “It was really on the way to crashing, and it was simply the resourcefulness of many people who took control of the co-pilot and neutralised him,” she said. The airline said it was another “on-duty flydubai crew travelling on the flight who diverted and landed the aircraft safely” and that it was suspending flights to Israel while an investigation took place. Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz alleged that the incident was an attempted terror attack, but did not identify his source of that assessment. The director general of Israel’s foreign ministry also called it “an attempted terrorist attack against Israelis, the United Arab Emirates, and the Abraham Accords”, referring to the normalisation deal the two countries signed in 2020. ‘Terrifying’ Passenger Almog Italie told AFP it was like “we were having very big turbulence” before fighting erupted near the cockpit. “The other passengers from the front took over control,” he told AFP via video call from Saudi Arabia. Passengers from an earlier diverted flydubai flight are seen after landing at Israel’s Ben Gurion Airport in Lod on September 30. – AFP Another passenger, Chaim Nazarovitz, said the ordeal had been “very terrifying”, adding that for a moment he felt like he was “not among the living”. Israeli media reported that the military scrambled fighter jets after concerns emerged that the aircraft might have been hijacked— with the hypothesis later dismissed. The incident comes months into a regional war that erupted in late February with US-Israeli strikes on Iran and just ahead of Israel’s elections due at the end of October. On Tuesday, Netanyahu said there were “indications” that Israel’s enemies could try to attack ahead of elections and was accused of “fear-mongering” by the opposition chief.

items.title: Nord-Ouest : six passagers enlevés à Babanki Tungo, la crise anglophone fait encore des victimes
items.description: © DR Six personnes viennent à nouveau d'être enlevées sur l'axe Bamenda-Ndop, l'un des corridors les plus dangereux du Nord-Ouest depuis l’enlisement de la crise séparatiste. Au compteur des exactions de la crise anglophone viennent encore de s’ajouter de nouveaux enlèvements. L'attaque s'est produite le mercredi 30 septembre 2026 vers 12h30 au niveau de Door Market, à Kedjom Ketinguh (Babanki Tungo). C’est dans l’arrondissement de Tubah, département de la Mezam, région du Nord-Ouest. D’après des sources locales, quatre véhicules de transport en commun en direction de Bamenda ont été interceptés par des hommes armés, reconnus comme des combattants séparatistes. Selon les mêmes sources, les passagers ont été dépouillés d'importantes sommes d'argent. Puis six d'entre eux ont par la suite été conduits vers une destination inconnue. Cet enlèvement n'est pas un fait isolé. Il porte la marque d'un conflit qui s'enracine. Et marqué entre autres par la récurrence des attaques sur le même axe. Le corridor Bamenda-Ndop-Kumbo est devenu comme une zone de non-droit où enlèvements contre rançon, extorsion et barrages illégaux sont quasi hebdomadaires. L'on note l’ancrage des chefs de guerre dans la zone qui reste sous le contrôle du chef séparatiste « General The Only Bro », régulièrement cité dans des enlèvements et assassinats de civils. Les opérations militaires n'ont pas encore réussi à le neutraliser. Aussi, il est à relever une réponse sécuritaire insuffisante. Comme à chaque attaque, habitants et transporteurs dénoncent le silence des autorités, aucune arrestation ni opération de sauvetage n'a encore été annoncée publiquement après les faits. Les opérations des séparatistes ne sont menées dans le sens des affrontements Armée contre séparatistes. Mais elles sont des attaques systématiques contre des civils désarmés pour financer la guerre par la rançon. Dix ans que cela dure. Tous les espoirs sont tournés vers un retour définitif à la paix. items.title: Cameroun/ Climat : 8 448 hectares de terres dégradées à restaurer dans le Nord et l’Extrême-Nord
items.description: © DR Un atelier de validation du document du Projet GEF-8 intitulé : « Gestion intégrée des paysages, utilisation durable de la biodiversité et résilience à la sécheresse dans les Régions du Nord et de l'Extrême-Nord du Cameroun » a eu lieu à Yaoundé le 29 septembre 2026. Les travaux, ouverts par le ministre en charge de l'Environnement, ont réuni plusieurs parties prenantes nationales ainsi que les représentants de la FAO et du Fonds pour l'environnement mondial (FEM). L’objectif de ces assises était d’examiner, finaliser et valider le document du projet en vue de sa soumission au FEM. Au cœur du projet se trouve la restauration de 8 448 hectares de terres et de paysages dégradés dans les deux régions septentrionales, fortement touchées par la désertification et la sécheresse. Le projet prévoit également de placer 11 933 hectares de terres agricoles et de pâturages sous une gestion durable et intelligente face à la sécheresse. Contribuer à l'atténuation de 1 020 800 tonnes de CO2. Atteindre au moins 8 150 bénéficiaires directs, dont au moins 50% de femmes. À travers une approche intégrée, cette initiative entend contribuer à la restauration des écosystèmes, à la préservation de la biodiversité et au renforcement de la résilience des communautés face aux changements climatiques. items.title: Crise anglophone : la saisie de 707 supports »ambazoniens » à Ekok illustre la persistance des velléités séparatistes
items.description: © DR 670 T-shirts, 32 toiles et 5 drapeaux ''ambazoniens'' ont été interceptés à la frontière. Une saisie qui, dix ans après son déclenchement, dit tout de la persistance de la crise anglophone. Ce mardi 29 septembre 2026, la Brigade commerciale des Douanes d'Ekok a intercepté sur l'axe Nigeria-Cameroun un véhicule transportant un important matériel de propagande séparatiste. Dissimulé dans la cargaison, le stock était destiné à alimenter les réseaux du Nord-Ouest et du Sud-Ouest, les deux régions camerounaises en proie à la crise sécessionniste depuis 2016. Loin d’être le fruit d’un simple contrôle douanier, cette interception est un marqueur. Elle confirme que la chaîne logistique transfrontalière des groupes armés reste active, et que la guerre, entrée dans sa 10e année, est loin d'être éteinte. Et ce, malgré les efforts des pouvoirs publics, la fragilisation progressive des donneurs d’ordre et financiers des groupes armés séparatistes ainsi que la tendance baissière des violences. C’est pourtant en fin octobre 2016 que tout part d'un mouvement d'humeur d'avocats et d'enseignants anglophones à Bamenda et Buea pour défendre le Common Law et le sous-système éducatif anglophone. La répression est brutale. Fin 2017, la contestation mute en conflit armé avec la proclamation de la République autoproclamée d'Ambazonie. Dix ans plus tard, malgré le Grand Dialogue national de 2019 et le Statut spécial accordé aux deux régions, le corridor Ekok-Bamenda, par où vient d'être saisi ce matériel, reste l'une des principales artères d'approvisionnement des séparatistes en propagande, armes, composants d'engins explosifs improvisés (EEI) et Tramadol. Le 29 septembre, deux jours avant le 1 er octobre, jour anniversaire de la réunification du Cameroun méridional sous administration britannique au Cameroun français indépendant, la persistance des véléités séparatistes se lit dans les chiffres. Plus de 6 000 morts selon l'ONU et International Crisis Group ; plus de de 700 000 déplacés dont près de 584 000 internes.
